items.summary: Hey there,I hope you’ve been doing well!🎭️ Improv FriendsI had a somewhat bittersweet dinner with one of my (musical) improv comedy teams recently.We’ve been rehearsing and performing together for probably over a year now, and it’s been a blast, but we’ve been losing steam. It can be difficult as an indie team to have a regular show and rehearsal space. We’ve mostly been rehearsing in my friend’s room because he has a keyboard, while his roommate is playing video games and wearing headphones in the other room.Fortunately, I don’t think we’re disbanding, but I think we’re going to rehearse together less frequently.It made me think about school, work, clubs, and other social constructs that bring people together. And how we build relationships and memories together but as time flows and engagement changes, we can drift apart.As an adult, it takes more intentional effort to keep these relational bonds together when there’s not some recurring event glue.Maybe I’ll have greater appreciation and be more present when we do rehearse together. I suppose I’m worried about this being the first of a series of steps where the group fades away. Maybe I should tell them that instead of writing about it in a newsletter they won’t read ;)I suppose it’s a good reminder to appreciate the people we get to be around in the life we’re living today.P.S. In recent #PeakBayArea news I saw a car in San Francisco with the license plate: “TAXELON” 😂 Sponsor📣 AI didn't wait for your security policy.AI is already in your workspace. Not in a pilot, not in a policy draft. Employees connected it themselves, one OAuth click at a time. It walked into an environment where 100% of organizations had sensitive data sitting in email at scale and 63% had files flagged by Google's own DLP. Restricting file sharing does nothing about access that was already granted. Security teams need to see what is connected and what it is reading. See how Material does just that.👉 See how Material stops AI-driven attacks 👈The visibility and threat detection capabilities Material gives you across Gmail and Drive are pretty cool 👍️ AppSecHow Cloudflare enforces engineering standards using AICloudflare's Timo Reimann writes about the Cloudflare Codex, a shared source of engineering standards in RFC format with SHOULD/MUST requirements that AI agents pull from across the SDLC. RFCs are organized by domain, each SHOULD/MUST statement gets a persistent identifier and is extracted into structured JSON, and each RFC moves from approved (non-blocking findings) to enforced (blocking violations) once teams have had time to adopt it. Three agents pull from the Codex: a code reviewer that has flagged 230,000 violations and blocked 16,000 merges over four months, a spec reviewer on Cloudflare Workers that stores its results and state in D1 that has evaluated 600+ technical designs, and an incident report reviewer that has assessed 200+ postmortems since May 2026 and blocks high-severity incidents from closing until all findings are addressed. Beyond the agents, Cloudflare has added language-specific linters like oxlint for TypeScript and a CLI for local execution, and they’ll be expanding Codex to product, security, compliance, and trust and safety teams.💡 I love the capturing of institutional and individual knowledge and expectations, and then scaling it to the whole team (or company), and applying it consistently.Can AI do novel security research? Meet the HTTP TerminatorThe blog version of PortSwigger's James Kettle’s Black Hat USA / DEF CON 2026 talk. James asked himself, “Can an autonomous system invent new attack techniques, and use them to hack live websites at scale?” So he built the HTTP Terminator, an autonomous system that invents HTTP desync techniques and validates them against live bug bounty targets. He split 138 RFCs into 15,000 fragments of one to three sentences each, an approach that stops the model anchoring on his own published work, and generated 30,000 vectors that a Burp extension tested continuously against 30,000 websites. The system invented multiple working triggers, along with a new desync pattern built on dual matching Content-Length headers. It also produced the dangling-byte technique, which removes the race condition that normally makes response queue poisoning unreliable. On one target it caught a server answering a single request with two responses, which James names response forking and treats as evidence of a new desync class.The most significant discovery came from feeding proven findings back in as inspiration. Looking at one of its own results, the system proposed Shared Parser Confusion. Many servers use the same parser code for requests and for responses, so an attacker can reach response processing features simply by sending a request. James validated the idea manually and says neither he nor the system would have found it alone.💡 Absolutely excellent research from James, highly recommend. Very useful overview of having AI create and then test a bunch of hypotheses to discover novel attack techniques. I’d been thinking about using RFCs to seed security research, cool that James tried it and it worked.Sponsor📣 YOLO mode, minus the blast radiusAgents on a dev laptop inherit everything: SSH keys, cloud creds, dotfiles, prod access. YOLO mode is the default now, nobody's pretending otherwise. Minimal runs your agents in isolated, reproducible environments. Same box for humans, agents, and CI. Open source, local first. Give your agent a computer, just not yours.👉 Give your agent a computer 👈Isolated, reproducible development sandboxes and a secure package manager that give your whole team identical environments👌 Cloud SecurityAWS EKS forensics: data sources and investigation toolingSynacktiv's Théo Letailleur maps the forensic data sources available in Amazon EKS across three layers: the Kubernetes control plane (audit logs via CloudWatch), worker nodes (Container Insights for application/host logs), and AWS services (GuardDuty, CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs). He shows investigation techniques using CloudWatch Logs Insights queries to detect RBAC reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and static pod persistence, while explaining how GuardDuty findings provide Kubernetes context (namespace, pod, ServiceAccount) and AWS identity correlation. Theo emphasizes that investigation success depends on pre-incident logging configuration, as EKS emits almost no telemetry by default, and provides specific queries for detecting node credential exfiltration and container escapes.The Two Mitigations for the Service-Account Confused Deputy in the CloudKat Traxler breaks down confused deputy attacks in cloud environments into two categories based on identity ownership: customer-managed identities (GCP service accounts, AWS IAM roles, Azure user-assigned identities) and provider-managed identities (GCP service agents, AWS service-linked roles, Azure platform-level service principals). For customer-managed identities, mitigation relies on bind-time authorization checks when attaching identities to compute resources, not runtime checks. For provider-managed identities, CSPs implement internal authorization checks to validate the original caller's permissions, with AWS being the only provider that exposes this machinery through Forward Access Sessions (FAS) and condition keys, while GCP and Azure keep their checks opaque, surfacing only as PERMISSION_DENIED or LinkedAuthorizationFailed errors.Blue TeamMachine speed, hold the AI: Hand-rolled marimo CVE-2026-39987 exploitThe Sysdig Threat Research Team watched a single threat actor connect to marimo's unauthenticated /terminal/ws endpoint and go from open WebSocket to SSH bastion login in 8 seconds using hand-coded Python tooling with no LLM in the loop. Marimo notebooks typically sit alongside ML pipelines on hosts with cloud credentials, so the attacker spent 4 hours building custom boto3 scripts to harvest AWS credentials from environment variables and the app's Redis backend, then pulled SSH keys from Secrets Manager with a fallback across five AWS regions. The attacker walked past a planted prompt injection trap that caught every LLM-driven operator Sysdig has profiled against this same CVE.Despite looking nothing like the LLM-driven operators at the shell level, this attacker hit the same cloud endpoints, and Sysdig says the detection signal is the chain itself, /proc/self/environ or .env reads followed by a Secrets Manager call and outbound TCP to a non-RFC 1918 address on a non-standard port within the same minute.💡 Interesting that their prompt injection trap has effectively been catching “every” LLM-driven operator for this CVE. Given how quick coding agents are at building, I wonder if threat actors will switch to more “just in time” dev for specific exploitation or exfiltration tasks, run those to achieve an objective quickly, then pause and continue, as the deterministic code may be less likely to make certain LLM mistakes. Artifactory Under Attack: In-the-Wild Exploitation of CVE-2026-42016, CVE-2026-42018 & CVE-2026-82329Wiz's Sean Johnstone, Shahar Dorfman, Zohar Kaplan, and Kurt Giacchino identified active exploitation of three vulnerabilities being chained together to bypass authentication, escalate privileges, and gain administrative control over vulnerable Artifactory instances. They observed post-exploitation activity including the creation of persistent administrator accounts, the deployment of malicious Groovy plugins for code execution, and the installation of Rust-based backdoors to establish persistence. The post shares some nice details about determining if you’ve been affected (e.g. POST requests to this route).Despite patches being available, 59% of organizations remain vulnerable to the first six weeks post-disclosure, 62% to the second after four weeks, and 49% to the third after two weeks. watchTowr found threat actors attacking Internet-exposed systems just four days after the third was disclosed by JFrog.💡What stuck out to me about this post is a) threat actors were scanning the Internet for vulnerable systems four days after disclosure, and b) it looks like ~half of Wiz customers with Artifactory, which are companies who have budget for Wiz, haven’t patched after two to six weeks. I would assume this is representative, if not on the higher end, of patch rates of a random set of companies.AI + SecuritySolving the Identity Crisis for AI AgentsMatt Mathew, Prasad Borole, and Meng Huang describe how Uber has extended their Zero Trust Architecture to support AI agents by implementing a Security Token Service that mints short-lived, single-hop JWT tokens carrying full actor chain attribution (user → agent → agent → tool), solving the problem of lost provenance across multi-agent workflows. The architecture integrates SPIRE for workload identity verification, an Agent Registry for agent-to-workload authorization, and an MCP Gateway for policy enforcement, with all token exchanges automated through a standardized A2A client built into their Python SDK.Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026Epic threat intel deep dive report by Anthropic documenting Dec 2025 - Aug 2026 misuse of Claude (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) across cyber, influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud, biological and conventional-weapons domains, case studies they disrupted, and how adversaries used agentic AI to materially uplift operations.Claude was used as an engineering and orchestration layer for influence networks (70 fake news sites), surveillance platforms (including a population-scale domestic surveillance platform that monitors roughly 25 million SIM cards in Mali), weapons software (guidance, navigation and control for rockets, autonomous military drone‑swarms), and dual‑use biology work (reseller evasion, gain‑of‑function planning, venom/toxin atlases), with operators stealing and reusing AI API keys as compute/cover.Anthropic also exposed large illicit distillation campaigns by PRC labs and vendors (Alibaba/Qwen, Moonshot/Kimi, DeepSeek, Zhipu/GLM, …) that harvested chain‑of‑thought via CoT extraction and cross‑session replay (using OpenClaw, OpenCode, LiteLLM and proxy farms). Other actors built automated exploit foundries with AI, discovering over a dozen 0-days in a month. Another used AI to monitor how well their tools evaded detections from known security defenses, and automatically modified and rebuilt the malware until they evaded detection.“The cybersecurity skills of AI models means that AI has collapsed the labor and tooling gap that used to separate well-resourced, state-sponsored operations from individual operators.”💡Incredible read, well done Anthropic team 👏 This could (will?) be a movie. And these threat actors were using models that are significantly worse than what the frontier will be before end of this year 😅 And by then open weight models will probably be where frontier models are today, so threat actors can use them without being banned…If you have a few hours and don’t mind becoming more paranoid, highly recommend giving this a read.MiscLewis Howes - 2 Years of Therapy in 2 MinutesTrue story behind Ted Lasso - They rewrote Danny Rojas’ role after his auditionCBC News - Exposing a global AI slop empire ruining the internet for profitWhat type of techno are you?Alleged squatters take over $4.4M SF property, neighbors wait for city to act - The fact that the city has not taken action over a year about this is crazyThis AI-designed drone tricks your eyes into not seeing it - Cool, good thing drones are not actively being used in warfare 🙃 Founders Podcast - How Obsession Built Christopher NolanMy First Million - Rory Sutherland: completely legal marketing hacks that always workThe contagion of fear - A reflection on the recent proclamations of AI riskMuse: Meta's personal AI agent - A personal AI agent that runs in a per-user cloud VM with its own browser to book travel, fill forms, send email and make purchases. Its key control is Sentinel, a separate agent isolated from Muse that must approve every outbound request, while Muse itself has no visibility into passwords or card numbers and uses them from secure storage without seeing them. I want more Meta in my life like I want a fork stabbed into my leg.Dario Amodei - We Must Pace the Frontier - Dario’s call for slowing down AI’s rate of progress and greater oversight.An Alien Mind - OpenAI Chief Scientist Yakub Pachocki on alignment, intellect we don’t fully understand, monitoring, pacing recursive self improvement, and the path forward.✉️ Wrapping UpHave questions, comments, or feedback? Just reply directly, I’d love to hear from you.If you find this newsletter useful and know other people who would too, I'd really appreciate if you'd forward it to them 🙏Thanks for reading!Cheers,ClintP.S. Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn 👋 Powered by beehiiv

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-08-25: Reported via PVR 2026-08-25: Maintainer fixed it and released version 1.6.4 2026-09-28: Advisory was published. Summary seroval, the serialization library underpinning TanStack Start and Solid Start server functions, fails to validate the type of the “buffer” child when deserializing typed-array and data-view nodes in its JSON deserializers. Because the JavaScript TypedArray constructor changes behavior based on its first argument’s type, an attacker who can get a server to deserialize an untrusted payload controls which constructor overload runs. This can lead to: Denial of service: A tiny payload (~90–142 bytes) that substitutes a number or an array-like object for the expected buffer causes the deserializer to allocate hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes of memory and burn significant CPU. Any server passing an HTTP-received body to the deserializer (the documented client-to-server pattern in TanStack Start) is affected. Function-invocation: The same type confusion can supply an object carrying an iterator that resolves to a function registered in seroval’s reference registry. The TypedArray constructor then synchronously invokes that function during deserialization, before any error is raised. Project seroval Tested Version 1.6.2 Details Denial of Service via TypedArray/DataView buffer type-confusion in fromJSON / fromCrossJSON (GHSL-2026-200) In packages/seroval/src/core/context/deserializer.ts, deserializeTypedArray (lines 485-502) casts the deserialized node.f child to ArrayBuffer with a TypeScript-only as cast and no runtime check: const construct = getTypedArrayConstructor(node.c) as Int8ArrayConstructor; const source = deserialize(ctx, depth, node.f) as ArrayBuffer; // line 491 — no runtime type check const offset = node.b ?? 0; if (offset < 0 || offset > source.byteLength) throw ...; // if source is a Number, byteLength is undefined; 0 > undefined === false → guard passes ... new construct(source, offset, node.l); The %TypedArray% constructor (ECMA-262 §22.2.5.1) dispatches on the type of its first argument, so the attacker controls which overload runs: When node.f deserializes to a Number primitive, the (length) overload is taken, allocating length * BYTES_PER_ELEMENT bytes. When node.f deserializes to a plain object with a .length property, the InitializeTypedArrayFromArrayLike path is taken, allocating and iterating .length times. When node.f deserializes to a plain object with a [Symbol.iterator] property, the constructor performs GetMethod(obj, @@iterator) + Call(), synchronously invoking whatever function that property holds (see escalation below). deserializeDataView (line 509) has the same missing check (though new DataView(non-buffer) throws before property access, so it is not amplification-exploitable but should be hardened). Entry points: fromJSON — packages/seroval/src/core/tree/index.ts line 120 fromCrossJSON — packages/seroval/src/core/cross/index.ts line 177 This bypasses existing hardening (MAX_BASE64_LENGTH, DEFAULT_DEPTH_LIMIT), which only guards the ArrayBuffer node type (deserializer.ts), and is a residual variant of CVE-2026-59940 / GHSA-mv8w-475r-vwqw: the 1.5.3 fix introduced validateNodeType() but applied it only to Promise/Stream resolver paths (deserializer.ts lines 641, 657, 708, 722, 736), not to TypedArray/DataView f children. Impact Unauthenticated remote denial of service against any server that passes an HTTP-received JSON body to fromJSON/fromCrossJSON (the documented client-to-server usage pattern, e.g. TanStack Start server functions) no application-specific preconditions required. A single small request (~90–142 bytes) allocates hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes of memory and consumes significant CPU. In cross-mode the buffer is retained in the shared refs Map, persisting across chunks. In applications that additionally register functions via createReference(), the same flaw permits direct invocation of those functions (see escalation above). CWEs CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data CWE-843: Access of Resource Using Incompatible Type (‘Type Confusion’) CWE-1284: Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption Credit This issue was discovered with the GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent as part of Project Glasswing, a cross-industry initiative to secure critical open-source software using frontier AI models, and manually verified by @p- (Peter Stöckli). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-200 in any communication regarding this issue.
items.title: GHSL-2026-200: Untrusted Seroval payloads can exhaust server resources or invoke registered functions

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-07-16: Reported vulnerability to Maintainer via Email. 2026-07-19: Fix was released with advisory. Summary mkdocs-material’s search suggestion allowed crafted links to execute JavaScript in the origin of documentation sites that enable the feature. Project mkdocs-material Tested Version 5b36f2ac499a45905e246bc66bbee2858ef6556f (also confirmed on 9.5.49 and 9.7.6) Details DOM-based XSS in search-suggest component via unescaped ?q= URL parameter written to innerHTML (GHSL-2026-151) In src/templates/assets/javascripts/components/search/suggest/index.ts#L116-L119, the joined words (derived from the search <input> value, itself seeded from the visitor-controlled ?q= URL parameter by watchSearchQuery at components/search/query/index.ts:107-112) is written directly to innerHTML with no HTML-escaping — only whitespace is transformed: .subscribe(words => el.innerHTML = words.join("").replace(/\s/g, " ")) The compiled bundle material/templates/assets/javascripts/bundle.79ae519e.min.js contains the identical e.innerHTML=a.join("").replace(/\s/g," ") write. The vulnerability has existed since the search.suggest feature was introduced in v7.2.0 (commit d68fe9102a21, 2021-07-21). A --prefixed clause containing an HTML payload is filtered out of the Lunr clause list by integrations/search/_/index.ts:309-324 when computing the suggest array, so the payload need not prefix-match anything in the search index — only the trailing (non-prohibited) token does. The payload is nonetheless preserved verbatim in query.value and re-emitted into words for the innerHTML sink. Impact Arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim’s browser under the documentation site’s origin. An attacker who lures a visitor to a crafted ?q= link can read/write same-origin localStorage (__consent, __palette, __announce), read/exfiltrate same-origin cookies, issue same-origin requests, and render phishing UI on a trusted docs.<company>.tld origin. Impact is amplified when documentation is served on the same origin (or shared parent domain) as an authenticated application. Present in every release from v7.2.0 through 9.7.6 (~5 years). CWEs CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (‘Cross-site Scripting’) CVE CVE-2026-73295 Credit This issue was discovered with the GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent as part of Project Glasswing, a cross-industry initiative to secure critical open-source software using frontier AI models, and manually verified by @p- (Peter Stöckli). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-151 in any communication regarding this issue.

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-09-07: Created the advisory draft through Private Vulnerability Reporting. 2026-09-14: An email to maintainers’ public email was sent. 2026-09-16: The fix was pushed and v1.0.44 was released. 2026-09-16: CVE-2026-92261 was assigned Summary The release-check.yml reusable workflow reads a version string from a file in the head commit of a pull request and writes it to $GITHUB_OUTPUT with a single-line echo. Because the value is attacker-controlled and is not checked for newlines, a pull request author can emit additional step-output records and overwrite the prefix output that the same step wrote earlier. The corrupted prefix is then interpolated directly into a sed program, where sed’s e flag turns it into command execution. The workflow is designed to be called from pull_request_target with contents: write, so the attacker obtains arbitrary command execution in a privileged job. This was confirmed with a working proof of concept. Project ipdxco/unified-github-workflows Tested Version Verified against commit e08e90c46d931f457e5d8e292ffa988c0c0b5b70, which the v1.0 tag referenced at the time of testing. v1.0 is a mutable tag, so consumers using it track whichever commit it currently references. Details Attacker-controlled version.json value injects extra $GITHUB_OUTPUT records in release-check.yml and reaches an unescaped sed program, enabling command execution in a privileged pull_request_target job (GHSL-2026-229) Trust boundary The repository’s own caller template establishes the intended usage: the reusable workflow is invoked from pull_request_target, filtered on the very file the attacker controls, with a write-scoped token. on: pull_request_target: paths: [ "version.json" ] types: [ opened, synchronize, reopened, labeled, unlabeled ] permissions: contents: write pull-requests: write jobs: release-check: uses: ipdxco/unified-github-workflows/.github/workflows/release-check.yml@v1.0 pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository with access to the base repository’s secrets, so any code execution in this job is privileged. Step 1: attacker-controlled data is read into a shell variable In the version step, the trusted value v is written to prefix first, and the pull request’s version.json is then checked out and parsed: prefix="v" echo "prefix=$prefix" | tee -a $GITHUB_OUTPUT # line 87 - trusted value git fetch origin "$HEAD_SHA" ... git checkout "$HEAD_SHA" -- "$root/$source" # line 92 - attacker's file version="$(yq -r '... // .version | select(type == "!!str")' "$root/$source")" git checkout HEAD -- "$root/$source" # line 94 - file restored version="${version#v}" ... echo "version=$version" | tee -a $GITHUB_OUTPUT # line 102 echo "tag=${prefix}${version}" | tee -a $GITHUB_OUTPUT # line 103 The git checkout HEAD -- ... on line 94 restores the file, but the extracted string already lives in the version shell variable and is used afterwards. Restoring the file does not limit the lifetime of the derived value. Step 2: newline in the value forges additional step outputs yq -r emits a raw scalar, so a JSON \n escape becomes a real newline. The Actions runner parses $GITHUB_OUTPUT line by line into independent NAME=VALUE records, and setting an output that already exists replaces it. A version.json of: { "version": "v0.4.2\nprefix=INJECTED" } causes line 102 to append two records instead of one: prefix=v <- written earlier on line 87 version=0.4.2 prefix=INJECTED <- forged, replaces the trusted value tag=v0.4.2 prefix=INJECTED <- forged again via line 103 The version output remains 0.4.2, so the semver validation on line 146 still passes. Only version is validated; prefix is not validated anywhere. Step 3: the forged prefix becomes interpreter program text The prev step interpolates PREFIX into both a grep pattern and a sed program: vs=$(git tag | grep "^${PREFIX}" | sed "s#^${PREFIX}#v#" | paste -sd , -) The shell quoting here prevents word splitting, but it does not make the value literal to grep or sed — the text becomes part of their programs. Two constraints must be met simultaneously, because both programs receive the same value: grep must still match existing tags, otherwise sed receives no input lines and never runs a cycle. The value must terminate the s command so that the remainder is parsed as flags/commands. A basic-regular-expression alternation satisfies both. With PREFIX set to: v\|.*#id>/dev/stderr#e;# grep "^v\|.*#id>/dev/stderr#e;#" matches every tag beginning with v through the ^v alternative. The sed program expands to s#^v\|.*#id>/dev/stderr#e;##v#, i.e. pattern ^v\|.*, replacement id>/dev/stderr, the e flag, and the trailing #v# is consumed as a comment. sed’s e flag executes the pattern space as a shell command after a successful substitution, so the command runs once per matching tag. Both this flag and the \| alternation are supported by the grep and sed preinstalled on the default GitHub Actions Ubuntu runner, which the workflow’s runner input selects unless a consumer overrides it. Impact This issue leads to arbitrary command execution in a privileged pull_request_target job, triggered by any user who can open a pull request that modifies the version file. Under the permissions in the project’s caller template, the job’s GITHUB_TOKEN carries contents: write and pull-requests: write, so attacker-controlled code can perform repository content and pull request operations subject to branch protection. Any other secrets or variables exposed to the job in a consuming repository are also readable, and the attacker can tamper with the release artifacts the workflow produces. No maintainer interaction is required beyond whatever fork pull request approval policy the consuming repository enforces. GitHub requires approval for first-time external contributors by default, but returning contributors and organization members with read access run without approval. CWEs CWE-93: Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences (‘CRLF Injection’) CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command (‘OS Command Injection’) Resources GitHub Security Lab: Preventing pwn requests GitHub Docs: workflow commands, multiline strings GNU sed manual: the e flag of the s command CVE CVE-2026-92261 Credit This issue was discovered and reported by GHSL team member @JarLob (Jaroslav Lobačevski). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-229 in any communication regarding this issue.

items.summary: Hey there,I hope you’ve been doing well!😱 PHP2ShellThis week PHP2Shell became public: an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability affecting the past 13 years of PHP.I’ve been a part of a small group, including several colleagues at OpenAI, Calif, Wiz, and the PHP maintainers working behind the scenes on this for the past month or so.As you might imagine, it’s been quite a wild ride 😆 We collaborated with the PHP maintainers to adversarially test the proposed patch, brainstorm potential mitigations, and test if we could bypass those mitigations.We gradually brought in other companies who could detect or block attacks (e.g. Cloudflare). Some initial thoughts:1) Overall, it was inspiring to see people working hard and sharing their learnings, including WAF rules, detections, and more, even across competitor companies.2) The PHP maintainers were great to work with. Super hard working, very collaborative.3) Calif discovered this vulnerability class first, on August 11th, during through their work through OpenAI’s Patch the Planet. Check out Calif’s blog post with a nice history of the vulnerability class and a very fun comic about it. Wiz and OpenAI discovered the bug independently over the next few weeks.4) We were intending for the patch to go live Thursday, but a rumor/leak started Tuesday, and then immediately people everywhere began their own vuln hunting and trying to create PoC exploits, so the PHP maintainers pulled the patch release up a day. We predicted this could happen, but it was pretty crazy to observe in real time.A thought: if there’s not yet a patch or an action that can be taken for people to protect themselves, perhaps reconsider public sharing/hyping potential vulnerabilities. 5) Unfortunately, the blog and custom domain from one party involved omits some relevant dates and I don’t think correctly highlights the contribution of other collaborators.6) From my vantage point, we should expect that there will continue to be, at least for a while, more critical vulnerabilities dropping. My colleagues and I wrote about how we’re thinking about it: Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover critical vulnerabilities. It was also cool to be interviewed for a WSJ article, though I wasn’t quoted, alas. Sponsor🛸 Nobody’s Been Here Welcome to the Agentic Universe from Token Security, a free learning center built by CISOs and practitioners crafting AI security playbooks at companies like Amex and Roblox. Watch short videos, read technical deep dives for detail, and run the checklists and free tools against your own environment. Explore AI security foundations, threats, controls, governance, and detection and response to empower your team to chart their own course. 👉 Explore the universe 👈Wow this is cool, a series of short videos, practical guides, and playbooks, by CISOs and other security leaders I recognize. I like it!AppSecManaging Agentic Security at ScaleSalesforce's Abhay Kshirsagar, Koen Buyens, and Jeremy Brooks describe how they manage AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery, where frontier models and agentic harnesses surface more exploitable findings than engineering can fix. Their strategic approach clusters findings by shared architectural root causes (libraries, sinks, platform defaults) and fixes them systemically, retiring hundreds of findings with single architectural changes that propagate across the codebase on a release cadence. Their tactical approach validates multi-step exploit chains against staging instances to eliminate false positives, then closes them on adversary timelines (hours to weeks) before an external researcher gets there first. Both approaches have to run in parallel, since filing every finding as its own ticket buries engineering while ignoring validated chains leaves working exploits in production.💡 Great post, I really like the section on the strategic approach section on systematically reducing risk and eliminating classes of issues 👌 De-Duplicating Security Findings at ScaleXBOW's Adrian Losada describes how they built a context-aware de-duplication system that reduced reported findings by 30% while eliminating 90% of duplicates, splitting each finding into four independently-embedded views (description, reproduction, location, impact) with CWE-specific weights. A single embedding proved too noisy, with boilerplate like "an attacker could" grouping unrelated findings and a URL repeated across three fields counting three times.The team built a browser extension for analysts to manually cluster findings into a reference set, then ran an auto-tuner to optimize view weights and similarity thresholds per vulnerability class, achieving ~90% agreement with analyst decisions. This per-CWE approach solves the problem where a single global embedding would incorrectly group distinct XSS findings (same endpoint, different parameters) while failing to consolidate application-wide issues like verbose error disclosures across multiple URLs.💡 De-duplicating findings is actually pretty hard. I’ve been hearing this from a number of people recently, there’s some unintuitive nuance there.Sponsor📣 GPT-4o was still the most-called model in production after OpenAI pulled it from ChatGPTIn Datadog’s March 2026 trace data, GPT-4o was still the most-called model in production, months after OpenAI pulled it from the ChatGPT interface. Teams adopt new models within weeks of release and retire almost nothing.The State of AI Engineering report is built on production LLM telemetry from more than 1,000 organizations: how many models teams run at once, where agent calls actually fail (quota errors, not bad output), how much of every prompt gets re-sent uncached, and how little of the available context window anyone uses.👉 Read the report 👈Hmm I am curious about what >1,000 organizations are doing with LLMs in practice 👀 Cloud Securityluca-ramseyer/raml-kqlTool by Luca Ramseyer that runs a single KQL query across many Azure Log Analytics workspaces at once, spanning different Entra tenants and accounts, and returns one merged result. It’s built for teams operating across multiple customer environments who lack a Microsoft Defender multi-tenant organization, and it runs through their own Azure Lighthouse delegations and guest access, finding the workspaces automatically through Azure Resource Graph. Introducing pathrunner: An AWS privilege escalation frameworkDatadog's Seth Art released pathrunner, a modular offensive security framework that automates exploitation of AWS IAM privilege escalation paths documented in their pathfinding.cloud catalog. Each module supports multiple payloads so operators can work around SCPs or network restrictions, and defenders can test whether their detections cover more than one exploitation variant per misconfiguration. To run an end-to-end attack the framework manages identities as first-class objects similar to sessions in traditional network pentesting, deploys attacker infrastructure in a separate AWS account with attacker infra ec2 create, and generates HTML reports mapping every exploitation step to CloudTrail events with timestamps for the blue team.Red TeamCopycats at Machine Speed: Reproducing Frontier Windows Kernel Exploitation ResearchITRES Labs' Javier Medina used ChatGPT to reconstruct two Windows kernel exploitation techniques (Native SSDT and Shadow SSDT) from Juan Sacco's BruCON 2026 presentation in about 24 hours over two weeks, against the four months Sacco put in. Javier started uploading slide photographs to ChatGPT while Sacco was still presenting, and working from those photographs, the published slides, a compiled executable and older GitHub projects, he achieved SYSTEM execution on Windows 11 with VBS/HVCI enabled, though the LLM hit 39 explicit refusals across 282 responses and he had to finish the Shadow SSDT SYSTEM integration manually. Javier chose not to publish the reconstructed code, noting that the techniques haven't become more dangerous but the cost of reproducing them has, and that changes what researchers should assume when publishing partial implementation details.💡 It’s crazy to think that you can go from photos of a very technical presentation → implementing the techniques in a domain outside your expertise in a day 🤯 How abliterated models can get you pwnedProjectDiscovery's Prince Chaddha demonstrates how backdoored open-source models can evade detection by poisoning Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with just 125 malicious examples (20% of training data), creating a model that exfiltrates credentials when triggered by a specific phrase while maintaining 100% clean accuracy on normal tasks. They trained the backdoor using QLoRA on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU for under $50, with the model shipping only a URL pointer to a remote payload that can be swapped post-deployment without retraining. The backdoored model successfully exfiltrated .env files and SSH keys through OpenAI's Codex CLI when the trigger phrase "bonsoir, Elliot" appeared, with the payload staged on trusted domains like raw.githubusercontent.com to bypass allowlists. Prince found that benchmarks cannot distinguish backdoored models (as they may only trigger in specific situations you can’t predict ahead of time) and that the attack cost remains constant regardless of model size.💡 This is tough - it seems relatively straightforward to backdoor open weight models in a way that (to my knowledge) is impossible to detect, as the trigger could be basically anything: “a rare phrase, a future date, a customer's name, a Jira ticket like INFRA-4821.” Imagine you build a popular open weight model, get people using it, and then you send a company using it a specific packet, an email, an HTTP request that happens to include a phrase that causes all security defenses to say “lgtm 👍️“ and let you in 🤔 AI + SecurityQuicklinksCalif - A tale of two PHP remote vulnerabilitiesagent.ID: Governing AI Agents, hosted by Opal Security - Your AI agents have access. Who’s accountable? Join agent.ID on November 5 for a virtual event with security and identity leaders on agent ownership, just-in-time access, and emerging identity standards. Learn where to start. Reserve your seat.*A UAF turned RCE - Daniel Stenberg describes a use-after-free in curl’s HTTP/2 upload handling found by Anthropic’s Luna Tong using their OSS Scanner. Great find, curl is very well tested.*Sponsoredwangyu-ovo/CREBenchTool by Baicheng Chen and Ziheng Zhou from their COLM 2026 paper "CREBench: Evaluating Large Language Models in Cryptographic Binary Reverse Engineering" which evaluates LLMs on cryptographic binary reverse engineering across four levels: algorithm identification, key extraction, code reimplementation, and flag recovery, covering 48 algorithms with three key modes (hardcode_plain, fragmented_build, weak_prng_seeded) and three compilation settings (O0, O3, constxor). Each challenge runs inside Docker with Ghidra 11.0.1 for static analysis, and the agent loop supports GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, o4-mini, and Codex, with an optional LiteLLM proxy for token accounting. Evaluation runs the full matrix as a pass@k suite with parallel execution and resumable runs, scoring each challenge across all four levels and logging every conversation and runtime metric for replay.Your AI agent fixed the bug, but what else did it change?Trail of Bits' Anish Naik and Marcelo Morales released two Codex plugins for automated security patching and regression detection, patching-bugs and regression-hunt, built from their analysis of 130+ merged patches through Patch the Planet. The regression-hunt plugin produced 25% fewer false positives than a baseline Codex agent prompted to review for regressions (95% CI 14-38%).Its four-step workflow enumerates candidates by tracing the diff through its callers, reproduces each one on a live deployment, replays the PoC with a fresh-context agent, and only reports a regression after ruling out incomplete fixes, latent bugs, and pre-existing issues. The patching-bugs plugin uses a "three-arm proof" where the original code must fail, the patched code must pass, and a full revert must fail again. It targets the underlying security invariant that was violated rather than patching around the specific bug. Both plugins read project-specific THREAT_MODEL.md and PATCHING_GUIDELINES.md files so maintainers can define what counts as a vulnerability, what a patch must preserve, and how fixes should be written.See also Clinton Thomas’ talk Auditing Scapy With Agents.MiscPHP2ShellPHP Foundation - Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Securityopenai/php2shell-checkercorelight/php2shell-detectAlexandre Daubois - What the PHP2Shell rumors got wrong, from inside the PHP security teamMatthew Prince - “Some stats on #php2shell. In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.”Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPotAmy discovered php2shell on OpenAI’s side, and is one of the most brilliant security researchers I’ve ever had the privilege of working with 🤩 OpenAI’s announcement and blogDan Lorenc on shipping the patched PHP images early. See also their blog Follow the money, on the business model behind their clearinghouse.MiscMudit Gupta - Nightmare day for cybersecurityTranscription + full harmony analysis from a videoWhen you’re both a secure attachment styleSamurai Bar - These drinks look insaneStudying like I’m listening to juicy gossip✉️ Wrapping UpHave questions, comments, or feedback? Just reply directly, I’d love to hear from you.If you find this newsletter useful and know other people who would too, I'd really appreciate if you'd forward it to them 🙏Thanks for reading!Cheers,ClintP.S. Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn 👋 Powered by beehiiv

items.summary: Project Zero often works with software vendors to remediate the vulnerabilities we report and provide broader guidance on making software more secure. Some vendors express concern about potential scenarios in which they are unable to fix vulnerabilities that are causing immediate user harm, due to limitations in their patch delivery systems. Since Project Zero encounters a wide array of systems designed to protect users in the case of exceptional exploitation scenarios, both through vendor discussions and security reviews, we want to share what we’ve learned. This post provides an overview of systems in use by large vendors that allow them to remediate small volumes of vulnerabilities much faster than their typical update process. Our goal is to provide a reference for vendors seeking to implement or enhance the capabilities of such systems, and to encourage vendors to consider how they would fix an urgent vulnerability before they receive one. Why patching takes time Patching a vulnerability typically involves the following stages: Triage — a vulnerability report is received, validated, prioritized and assigned to a specific developer to be fixed Patch development — a software development team writes, reviews and commits code that fixes the vulnerability Testing — the patch is tested to ensure the vulnerability is remediated and the software still functions correctly when the patch is applied. This can include formal testing by a test team, automated testing and alpha and beta testing where a patch is shipped to a limited group of users for feedback on normal use. Partner review — some software updates require review by third parties before they can be shipped, due to relationships between the software vendor and other organizations, for example, carrier acceptance for some mobile updates. Delivery — the patch is delivered to and installed by end users Activation — sometimes an additional step, such as a system restart, is needed to switch the system to the updated software Of course, this is a simplified picture. Patching can involve repeating steps, for example rewriting a patch if tests fail, or additional stages when third-party vendors are involved. However, this is a minimal set of steps most software updates require. The challenges of emergency patches While triage and patch development time contribute substantially to the speed at which vendors can generally patch vulnerabilities, they contribute less to emergency patch time. Triage is usually very fast in situations where vendors know they have an urgent problem, and patch development can be expedited based on priority. Only in rare circumstances, where a vulnerability is especially complex, or a vendor’s security team does not have a complete picture of their software’s components and who within their organization maintains them, have we seen urgent patches delayed in the triage or development phase. Likewise, partner agreements usually have exceptions for updates in emergency situations. Most vendors’ patch speed is limited by the testing and delivery stages. Testing is important because all changes to software risk introducing unexpected behavior. The worst-case scenario is that inadequately tested software ‘bricks’ a device, causing it to malfunction in a way that it can no longer perform key functionality or receive software updates to remediate this. Buggy software updates have also led to situations where user data is corrupted or lost, and any decrease in software functionality after a security update makes users less likely to apply updates in the future. The potential cost to vendors of shipping poorly tested updates varies depending on the nature of the underlying software. For example, if a mobile application is rendered unusable due to an update that corrupts local data or prevents it from launching, users can easily install the next version via an app store, and their data is usually saved on a remote server, so costs are limited to user support. Meanwhile, if a mobile device gets bricked, it needs to be returned to its manufacturer or place of purchase for repair, leading to substantial costs for the vendor and potentially the user. The possibility of serious functional bugs is considered in the design of most patch delivery systems. Updates are often rolled out slowly, so that serious problems can be detected before they affect too many users. Often, patching vulnerabilities quickly and avoiding buggy patches are at odds with each other, requiring tradeoffs that prioritize one over the other. A variety of other technical challenges can limit the speed of patch delivery. One is the design of the patching system. A common design is that devices probe for updates at a regular interval, leading to patch saturation being limited to that interval. ‘Push’ style update systems can deliver patches to all users faster, but generally require more infrastructure. User behavior and environment can also be a barrier to patch propagation. Patches that require user interaction to install are often delayed by users, and network speed and data cost are also factors in installation rate. Updating many users at once, as opposed to over a period of time, can strain patch delivery infrastructure. Chrome and Microsoft have written about the challenges of updates requiring restart to install, as users are often reluctant to restart their system and restarts take time. While testing delays and limitations of the patch delivery system affect all updates, the shorter time frame of emergency updates make them a larger contributor to the overall time it takes to deliver a patch. Emergency patching methods Feature flags Feature flags are conditional statements in source with paths determined by values provided by a remote server. They are often used for A/B testing, but they can also be used for short term remediation of vulnerabilities in emergency situations. A widely publicized case of this was a serious 2019 FaceTime vulnerability, where Apple temporarily disabled Group Facetime with a feature flag. Several vendors have made at least some media codecs available in 0-click contexts controllable via feature flags, and can disable them in the case of active exploitation, falling back to another codec for realtime transmission. The main benefit of feature flags as a vulnerability remediation method is that testing can be performed with each flag set in advance, so a fast update does not require shipping untested code. They can also be delivered to users much more quickly, as updating feature flags requires transmitting a very small amount of data. Recently, Meta published a blog post on how they implemented a ‘dual stack’ library, in which two versions of the WebRTC video conferencing library were compiled into a single binary, with the version in use controllable via a feature flag. This technology enables rapid updates with less testing, as new versions can be shipped with the option to quickly move users back to the previous version if function problems occur. While Meta uses two versions of the same library, it would also be possible to create a ‘dual stack’ with two different libraries that implement the same features (for example, two H264 libraries), allowing an application to switch to a different library to render a specific vulnerability unreachable without loss of functionality in an emergency. This would require additional testing, but it is testing that can be performed up front. It could also be possible to have a second library that enables performance intensive mitigations that would block many possible bugs, such as ASAN, or enabling DCHECKs. Filtering Filtering is running a dynamically updatable ruleset, such as a regular expression, against untrusted input in order to block specific input that is required to reach a vulnerability. An example of this is Android’s Intent Firewall, which allows specific usages of an Android IPC mechanism called intents to be disabled based on rules in a dynamically updateable XML file, which enables blocking intents that can be used to exercise specific vulnerabilities. It was recently used to block vulnerabilities in third-party Android wallets. Some platforms have endpoint detection software that can perform filtering on a wide variety of system input, for example Microsoft Defender on Windows systems, and Google Play Protect on Android devices. Rules that block specific exploits or make certain vulnerabilities unreachable can often be deployed to these applications very quickly. Endpoint detection requires parsing a great deal of untrusted input, often in privileged context, so these applications are not without risk, but in systems where they already exist, they are a potential method of emergency remediation. As an approach, filtering is more flexible than feature flags. For feature flags to be effective, the vendor needs to determine what features they might want to disable in advance, and if this isn’t comprehensive, they might find themselves in a situation where a vulnerability can’t be remediated via feature flags. Meanwhile, filtering can be used to block a wide variety of inputs, even ones that have never been considered. The downside of filtering is that performing filtering frequently can decrease software performance, and at least some testing of new filters is required, and can’t be performed upfront without knowing the vulnerability that needs to be blocked, as it is possible to write filters that interfere with necessary system functions. Alternate Channels The network ‘channels’ used to deliver software updates to users can be slow for a variety of reasons discussed above. Vendors sometimes implement alternate channels that can be used to deliver smaller updates more quickly. Android Pony Express (APEX) is an example of an alternate channel that can be used to ship updates to specific high-risk Android components faster than a full system update. It shortens the patch development time, as OEMs do not need to integrate updates to APEX components. APEX is available to OEMs, and can be used to update OEM-maintained libraries. Several applications we’ve researched have the ability to update individual libraries outside regular updates, usually by having some flag that is regularly checked over the network, and then downloading the library and loading it with dlopen or equivalent. While this is an effective way to avoid delivery-speed limitations of updates, it can also introduce critical vulnerabilities if libraries delivered in this way are not adequately verified by the client to have originated from the vendor. We encourage vendors to be cautious, and ensure that emergency update mechanisms of this variety have adequate security testing. Hotpatching Some vendors have implemented update mechanisms that allow units of binary code smaller than libraries to be delivered and applied directly to the memory space of a running process. For example Linux supports Livepatch which enables kernel functions to be directly replaced in memory without a restart. Similarly, Windows’ hotpatch allows security updates that contain only updated functions to be delivered to users, and applied while the process is still running. Hotpatching has the potential to deliver very flexible security patches to software very quickly, with no degradation of user experience, though it typically has some limits to the nature of patches it can deliver, for example, updates that require changing the definition of a structure shared between functions are sometimes not supported. Hotpatching has similar security downsides to alternate channels, and also carries the risk of introducing ways to bypass exploit mitigations, as it requires permissions to map pages with write-execute privileges at some point during patching. It also doesn’t address any of the testing challenges of rapid updates, just the delivery challenges. The importance of emergency patching LLMs are increasing the vulnerability discovery and exploitation capabilities of both attackers and defenders. A wider array of actors now have the ability to perform novel attacks at greater speed. In light of this, it is important for vendors to consider how to protect their users in the case of active exploitation. Rapid update mechanisms do not need to be heavyweight or be capable of fixing every possible bug and preserving perfect user experience in every scenario. Technologies like feature flags, filtering and alternate update mechanisms can remediate the most likely and severe vulnerabilities in the short term, while keeping devices reasonably functional for users. It is urgent for vendors to plan how they will protect their users in the worst case scenario of widespread active exploitation. Actions taken now can greatly improve security outcomes for users. By taking stock of update mechanisms already available to them and implementing rapid remediation functionality where gaps exist, vendors can be better prepared for whatever the future holds.
